graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: O/S Proj Exp (Macro in Asia)
description:
Financial markets play a vital role in economic growth and development. At the same time, financial volatility highlights the importance of central banks in conducting monetary policy and maintaining financial stability.

This course consists of two parts. The first reviews key concepts in monetary theory, including interest rates, money market equilibrium, and the dynamic AD-AS model. Students will develop an understanding of how monetary policy influences macroeconomic outcomes and economic stabilisation.

The second part focuses on monetary policy and the role of central banks. Students will examine monetary policy frameworks, the money supply process, policy instruments, transmission mechanisms, exchange rate policy, and the challenges of policy implementation.

Through SMU-X experiential learning, students will work on real-world projects with the Central Bank of Vietnam, applying economic theory to practical policy issues such as monetary framework modernization, financial market oversight, and exchange rate management. These projects strengthen critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and communication skills.

As an SMU-XO course, students will also participate in an immersive experience in Vietnam through guest lectures, interactions with local students, and business visits, enhancing their global awareness and cultural competence while fulfilling the Global Exposure requirement.

Teamwork forms a key component of the course and is assessed through group projects and peer evaluations.
tracks: PLE: Public Policy and Governance Track
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Empirical Economics
description: This course is designed to equip students with practical knowledge for analysing micro data. We will cover essential concepts for causal inference and widely-used econometric tools such as linear regression, matching, instrumental variable regression, difference-in-difference, regression discontinuity design. Students will also learn to use Stata software for data management and analysis.

name: Microeconomics 2
description: This course provides students with a foundational study of the concepts and theories underlying economic interactions in markets and public organisations. The approach combines economic intuition with a rigorous treatment of the concepts taught. Students will learn about public goods, externalities, monopoly and monopsony, and oligopoly. In addition, students will learn the tools to deal with decisions under risk and how asymmetries of information affect economic institutions. Finally, students are introduced the basic concept from Game Theory, which provides a rigorous treatment of strategic decision making. During the course, the applicability of these concepts to practical situations and their linkages to various economic electives will be discussed.
tracks: PLE: Public Policy and Governance Track

name: Macroeconomics 2
description:
This course is the second part of a two-course Macroeconomics sequence. The aim of the sequence is twofold. First, it is to introduce students to modern macroeconomic theory, in particular formal macroeconomic models built on microfoundations. Second, it is to develop a deep understanding of macroeconomic phenomena such as business cycles, long-term economic growth, and the process of economic development, as well as macroeconomic policy issues, such as the impact of fiscal and monetary policy on the economy and the design of a social security system or an unemployment insurance scheme.
This second part of the sequence first reviews the topics of consumption and savings, investment, and the labor market covered in ECON 112 (Macroeconomics 1) and enriches the analysis by considering the impact on consumption and investment decisions of (a) imperfections of the financial sector, for instance leading to the existence of credit constraints, (b) uncertainty, and (c) adjustment costs, as well as by introducing the flow approach to the labor market and using the search and matching framework to understand labor market data and policies. The course then introduces the notion of money and considers the role of financial intermediaries, which are then used to study the long-term impact of monetary policy as well as the role of banking supervision and macro-prudential regulation. The course finally studies business cycles and covers the measurement of cycles, reviews the main existing theories and their policy prescriptions, with a particular emphasis being put on severe recessions or depressions.
tracks: PLE: Public Policy and Governance Track

name: Infrastructure Econs & Policy
description: This course is designed to provide students with an understanding of the theory and practice of the economics of infrastructure provision, regulation, and policy. The first section of the course will deal with reform and governance in the infrastructure sectors and the rationale for privatization and public-private partnerships (PPPs). The theoretical component will cover the rationale for economic regulation, the choice of regulatory instruments, pricing and subsidies, design of markets, regulatory institutions and PPPs. The analysis of these issues will be applied to several infrastructure sectors including water, telecommunications and the internet, transportation, and electricity. The infrastructure sector is increasingly prominent on the sustainability agenda with the adoption of net-zero emissions targets by over 100 countries and large corporations. The course will also discuss policy options and challenges for the transition to net-zero emissions. Relevant case studies will also be used to illustrate the application of economic principles to policy in specific sectors and contexts.
areas: Public Pol and Public Mgmt Electives
tracks: PLE: Public Policy and Governance Track

name: Adv. Mathematical Methods
description: This course covers mathematical concepts and techniques that are useful for more advanced work in Economics and Econometrics/Statistics. The course covers elementary linear algebra, basic topology (introduction to metric spaces and the topology of Euclidean spaces), differentiation of vector functions, nonlinear programming and dynamic optimisation, and an introduction to complex analysis. Pre-requisite: Intermediate Mathematics for Economics

name: Monetary Pol. & Fin. Stability
description: This course aims to equip students with an understanding of the nature and impact of financial risk transmission. In particular, it examines the changing roles of the central banks in managing such risks. The course relates the central bank's monetary policy and prudential oversight of financial institutions to the maintenance of financial stability. An important focus of the course is the role of the central bank in a small open economy such as Singapore. The structures and vulnerabilities of these economies often call for a different approach to monetary policy and financial stability policy. Pre-requisite: Intermediate Macroeconomics, International Economics

name: Economic Dynamics
description: This course covers mathematical concepts and techniques that are useful for more advanced treatment of economic analysis. We pay special attention to concepts and machineries that allow us to describe the economic system of dynamics and analyze inter-temporal optimization of an economic agent. The topics which will be covered are: (1) Topology in the Euclidean Space; (2) Linear Algebra; (3) Multivariate Calculus (Differentiation and Integration); (4) Static Optimization; (5) Differential Equations; (6) Difference Equations; and (7) Dynamic Optimization. In addition, we offer a lot of economic examples which utilize the techniques this course covers. A good comprehension of the material covered in the course enables you to (1) understand the appropriate mathematical tools together with applications in economics; and (2) stand out among your peers.

name: Asian Monetary Policy
description: This course introduces students to outstanding policy debates in the monetary economics of Asia. Course approach is threefold. The course anchors sovereign and regional policy debates within the context of the latest theoretical advances in the open economy macroeconomics literature. Current topics include exchange rate flexibility, interest rate rules, discretionary targeting regimes, regional integration, monetary coordination, multi-country linkages, and prospective monetary union. Students are expected to follow debates as discussed in professional journals and by regional central banks. The course also encourages students to explore the political economy that underlies the creation and implementation of monetary policy in Asia. Students are expected to analyse and debate the applicability of policy options within the context of current political economy. Finally, the course enables students to contribute to the existing literature by requiring a rigorous paper that addresses an outstanding monetary policy issue in Asia. The aim of the paper is to prepare students for staff positions at central banks, multilateral development institutions, think tanks, investment banks or for places in top-tier graduate schools.

name: Research Methods in Economics
description: The Research Methods in Economics will train students to conduct economic research. It is a prerequisite for the Senior Thesis, as it offers checkpoints for students to develop their own proposals. During the course, students are expected to 1) read and critically evaluate suitable research papers, 2) refresh the methodology with a particular emphasis on practical applications to the topic of their interest, 3) propose and refine their research question suitable for a Senior Thesis. 4) learn the programming skills necessary for the data and computational analytics in the proposed Senior Thesis.

prerequisites.name: ECON107 & ECON104 & STAT102/COR-STAT1202/1203 & ECON101/111 & ECON102/112 & ECON203/234/235 & ECON118 - Pre-req

graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Senior Thesis
description: Students registered for the Senior Thesis are required to write a scholarly report of about 40 typed pages (including bibliography and appendices) on current economic issues, or on theory or methodology in economics based on their original research.

name: HEM Work-Study Elective
longName: Health Economics and Management Work-Study Elective
description: This course is a collaboration between SingHealth and SMU that helps train young professionals looking to enter the healthcare sector in Singapore. It will provide students with an invaluable opportunity to undergo a 6-month internship programme at SingHealth through which students can acquire first-hand experience and knowledge of the healthcare sector. It is open to all SMU students, but preference is given to students who have already declared Health Economics and Management as their second major.

name: Microeconomics
description: This course covers the main building blocks of modern economic analysis. It covers topics such as consumer behavior and the theory of demand; production, cost, and supply functions; choices under uncertainty; competitive equilibrium; monopoly, price discrimination, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, duopoly models; game theory; factor demands; general equilibrium theory and welfare economics; information theory; externalities and public goods.

name: Macroeconomics
description: This course is an introduction to the study of the economy as a whole at an advanced level. It presents the major theories concerning some of the most important questions in economics. Why do some countries grow while others do not? What cause recessions and booms? How does government policy affect GDP, unemployment, inflation and growth? Topics covered include: consumption, investment, inter-temporal choice, and the rate of interest; issues in monetary and fiscal policy; models of economic growth; business cycles, unemployment and search.

name: Macroecon. & Global Fin. Mkts
description: This course provides students with a foundational study of macro-economic concepts and theories necessary to understand and analyze the state and outlook of the global economy and their impact on financial markets. The role of monetary policy and exchange rate policy in managing interest rates, inflation and trade competitiveness will be discussed and the linkages to strategies for investment management will be highlighted. The global economy and its financial markets are keenly interconnected:  Expectations of growth and policy changes impact financial markets to the same extent that fluctuations in market prices influence growth and policies.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Fin Econ & Modeling Techniques
description: This research seminar covers applications of econometric techniques to the analysis of financial data. Models with special relevance to asset prices, interest rate processes and exchange rate determination are discussed. The course also covers models of conditional volatility, continuous time stochastic processes, analysis of high frequency data and event study methodology.

name: International Trade
description: This research seminar covers the traditional topics under the rubric of the pure theory of international trade and trade policy under perfect competition as well as under imperfect competition. Additional topics covered may include strategic trade policy; trade and growth; the political economy of trade policy determination; empirical analysis of trade theories and policy; theory of preferential trading areas.

name: International Monetary Econs
description: The objective of the course is to provide students with an introduction to international monetary economics at the graduate level based on the recent theoretical and empirical literature, as well as a number of cutting-edge international policy issues. The course will cover models of exchange rate determination, theories and evidence regarding spot and forward exchange market intervention, old and new open-economy macroeconomic models, traditional target-zone and currency-crisis models, choice of exchange rate regime issues, and some of the more recent emerging market crisis models. The course will also review the broad evolution of the international monetary system focusing on the nature of the international adjustment process under alternative exchange rate regimes, the recent growth of private cross-border capital flows and the current challenges facing the international monetary/financial system. The course will conclude with a brief discussion of the issues posed by ongoing efforts to strengthen financial and monetary cooperation in Asia.

name: Search & Match Models Lbr Mkt
longName: Search & Matching Models of the Labor Market
description: This is a seminar style course on the application of search and matching theory to the labor market. Students will learn how models of frictions are used to explain many of the observed regularities in the labor market, business cycle phenomena such as job and worker turnover, unemployment, and effects of government policy such as unemployment insurance. We will also look at how these models are suitably taken to data. We will also take a closer look at various ways of wage determination: posting, bargaining, and take closer looks into how jobs and workers actually meet. Finally we will consider models in marriage markets as a way to motivate how heterogeneous workers meet heterogeneous firms.

name: Public Economics
description: This research seminar covers the theory and evidence of both government taxation policy as well as government expenditure policy. Topics covered include tax incidence; excess burdens; optimal tax theory; the economic effects of taxation on labor supply and savings decisions; taxation and corporate behaviour; the theory of public goods; political economy; redistribution and social welfare policy; social insurance programs such as fully funded and unfunded social security systems; health care policy.

name: Economics
description: The course is designed to provide the students with an appreciation for both the micro and macro aspects of Economics. This course examines the choices that confront consumers and firms, the roles of government, and the various types of market structures. On a macro perspective, topics covered include the aggregate demand and supply models, the studies of economic fluctuations and long run growth, and fiscal and monetary tools.

name: Contemp Issues in Asian Bus
description:
The module consists of several topics on different aspects of China to be taught by different Professors. The topics include:

1. Chinese Economy: Past, Present & Future by Prof Hongbin Cai
2. Chinese Government, Business Environment and Economic Development by Prof. Li-An Zhou
3. Negotiation and Conflict Resolution in China by Prof Li Ma
4. Financial Market and Investor Protection in China by Prof Guohua Jiang
5. Innovation in China by Prof Cai Jian

name: Econometrics
description: This course covers the basics of regression methods applied to the analysis of economic data. It focuses on the fundamental assumptions in the setup of an econometric model, the estimation techniques (ordinary least squares and generalized least squares) and their properties under correct and incorrect assumptions (serial correlation, heteroscedasticity, omitted variable, multicollinearity and measurement errors), and the model diagnostics and selection methods. Both time series and cross section data are discussed. Basic knowledge in statistics, calculus and linear algebra is assumed.

name: Understnd Glob Econ & Fin Mkt
longName: Understanding the Global Economy and Financial Markets
description: This course equips participants with the ability to understand major economic indicators and decipher their implications for business decisions. Participants will be able to determine what factors and indicators affect and move financial markets and why, how to make informed corporate decisions in conjunction with market movements, and how to infer emerging trends from such information.

name: Advanced Econometrics
description: This course is a sequel to Econometrics. It covers advanced topics in estimation (maximum likelihood method and generalized method of moments), diagnostic techniques (portmanteau tests, residual based tests and heteroscedastic autocorrelation consistent methods), the analysis of stationary and nonstationary time series (unit root test and cointegration analysis), the analysis of panel data and the modeling of limited dependent variables.

name: Industrial Organization
description: This course introduces the modern theory of industrial organization. Industrial organization mainly studies firms and markets, and in particular explores commonly-observed strategic interactions among firms. The related topics include monopoly, oligopoly, cartel, implicit collusion, price discrimination, and many others. We analyze strategic actions taken by firms to compete or collude with other firms, or retain their market powers, and then we evaluate outcomes of their actions in markets.

name: Topics in Economic Development
description:
This course covers selected topics in economic development from a policy-oriented perspective. The main objective of the course is to encourage and equip students to address policy issues pertaining to economic development from a broad analytical perspective. Topics covered include: the determinants of economic growth; poverty and inequality; some recent empirical experiences of growth and poverty reduction; aid effectiveness; governance and corruption; international trade and integration; migration and outsourcing. 

The course will be organized around a set of workshops led by the professor. Students need to do the required reading before each class and are encouraged to be active participants in class. This participation entails asking questions, providing counter arguments, advancing alternative explanations and exploring policy implications. Class participation and discussion are integral parts of this course and the learning process. Accordingly, absence from class will be penalized. 

Based on class size, students will work, individually or in groups and present one or more of the assigned readings. These presentations will not only summarize the assigned papers but also draw out policy implications and discuss their weaknesses. Student presentations should be approximately 30 minutes, to be followed by questions and discussions of issues raised during the presentations. 

Each student will prepare a research paper about 15 pages in length (excluding references, data, tables and figures). Immediately before the mid-term recess, each student will submit a 2-3 page prospectus for this research which will be presented and discussed in the class on the 8th week. This prospectus should include the motivation, a synoptic review of the literature, the methods that will be employed and the data source if the paper is going to be empirical. Before the end of the term, students will make presentations based on the seminar papers. The research papers may address any research topic within the broader purview of economic development, but it is assumed that most papers will draw from the issues covered in the course.

name: Topics in Econometrics A
description:
In the first half of the course ‘Topics in Econometrics’, various limited and qualitative variable models will be covered. GAUSS will be used to program estimators typically used in practice for those models. Each week is devoted to one topic as listed in the following: 
1. Binary response 

2. Ordered discrete response 

3. Count response 

4. Censored response 

5. Duration analysis 

6. Multinomial choice 

The final topic ‘multinomial choice’ may not be covered if duration analysis requires 2 weeks. 

Evaluation will be based on a couple of HW’s analyzing small but real data sets, and possibly one final project. Lecture notes will be provided. The students are expected to bring their notebook PC’s to the classroom.

name: Topics in Econometrics B
description: This part of the course provides an overview of modern time series econometrics, covering a range of material in stationary and nonstationary time series, including trend determination, model selection, unit root and cointegration theory, long memory properties and time series decompositions. Students will be introduced to some practical time series forecasting methods. The goal of the course is to help students understand and carry out empirical research in time series and make accessible a wide and rapidly growing literature in econometrics and time series macroeconomics.

name: Economic Analysis
description: This module covers the principles of microeconomic and macroeconomic analyses, with particular reference to economic management and the financial markets. Our aim is to learn theories in order to apply them in analysis. Topics in microeconomics include supply and demand, competition and monopoly, externalities and the new IT economy. Topics in macroeconomics include growth, trade, cycles and the recent developments in the rational expectation theory.

name: International Macroeconomics A
description:
This course covers the following topics:
1. Neo Classical Macro Economics
2. The New-Keynesian Macroeconomics
3. International Financial Crises
4. The Traditional Open Economy Macro Model 
5. Current Accounts Dynamics

name: International Macroeconomics B
description:
This portion of the course covers several topics in International Macroeconomics. It will draw on several readings given below and possibly other articles of interest.
1. Structuralist models of the open economy
2. Non-traded good sector, services sector and land
3. Persistent Currency Appreciations
4. Differences in hours worked across countries
5. Why do more open economies have bigger governments?

name: Urban Economics & Policy
description: Urban economics is the discipline that lies at the intersection of economics and geography.  This course will explore the location decisions of households and firms, and shows how these decisions interact with government regulation and policy to cause the formation of cities of different size and shape. It will apply economic thinking to the tasks of analyzing urban growth, urban real estate markets and the urban transportation system, as well as evaluate government policies that impact on these markets.   We will also analyze the links between primary and secondary mortgage markets, securitization, and liquidity. The links between local real estate and related markets such as transportation and public finance will also be explored.

name: Topics in Game Theory
description: This course is designated to introduce the theory of resource allocation problem from the normative point of view. Particularly, we will focus on claims problems: when agents have claims on a resource that add up to more than what is available, how should he resource be divided? A primary example is the so-called bankruptcy problem. A firm goes to bankrupt. How should we divide its liquidation value among its creditors? We are going to introduce several methods to deal with this problem and formulate a number of \"fairness\" criteria. The objective here is to figure out differences among methods and study the implications of properties, singly or in various combinations.

name: Mathematics for Economics
description: This course is designed to arm you with the essential mathematical tools extensively used in microeconomics, macroeconomics and econometrics. It is expected to enhance your aptitude for mathematical proofs, an essential component of economic theory, and to provide an adequate comprehension of important concepts and theories widely used in economics, from Taylor expansions to fixed point theorems, optimization theories and dynamic systems. (Note: probabilities and statistics will be covered separately.) Throughout the course, you will hopefully find that math could be really useful, a bit more fun and a bit less scary than many usually think.

name: Microeconomics II
description: The course is the second part of a graduate level introduction to microeconomics.  The objective is to provide students with a thorough grounding in the analytical methods of microeconomics theory.  The course will focus on (a) General Equilibrium Theory, (b) Game Theory, and (c) Welfare Economics/Incentives.

name: Macroeconomics II
description: This course overviews empirical aspects of the modern macroeconomics.  Empirical methods for research and policy analysis are introduced for various models including real business cycles, permanent income hypothesis, asset pricing, indivisible labour, sticky prices, and idiosyncratic shocks.  It covers both calibration and estimation methods mainly but not restricted to linear solutions, and further extends to Bayesian analysis of dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models.

name: Macroeconomics II
description:
This course is the second part of a two-part sequence. The aim of this sequence is to provide students with an indepth knowledge of the macro-economy and of recent macroeconomic phenomena through the exposure to modern dynamic macroeconomic models. The sequence also addresses the impact of policies on growth and development, the labor market, the business cycle, and stability of the financial system. This course first considers the functions fulfilled by the financial sector and in particular financial intermediaries before considering financial
crises and associated policy issues. We then move on to considering business cycle data and theories, before concluding by considering the role of fiscal and monetary policy in managing the business cycle.

name: Econometrics II
description: This is an overview of time series econometrics, designed to introduce students to a range of material in stationary and nonstationary time series, including unit root and cointegration theory, state-space models, non-linear time series analysis, continuous time models, and Bayesian time series methods.

name: Applied Microeconometrics
description: This course lays out modern methods in empirical microeconomics with an emphasis on applications. The first half of this course mainly covers generalized method of moments, panel data models, and limited dependent variable models. The second half gives an overview of policy evaluation methods.

name: Topics in Microeconomic Theory
description: This course studies topics in the economics of information. The first part of the course will introduce the notion of contingent commodities and study insurance markets. The focus of this part will be on the problem of adverse selection. The second part of the course will introduce the problem of moral hazard. The last part of the course will look at the now standard model of liquidity insurance introduced by Diamond and Dybvig 1983.

name: Macro-foundation Asset Pricing
description: The course introduces students to the economic principles and models behind pricing and valuation of assets. Starting with Lucas tree model, it covers various consumption-based and production-based asset pricing models. The relationship between equilibrium or the absence of arbitrage opportunities and the existence of a system of \"state prices\" is established, and then all asset prices are shown to be portfolios of state prices. It also sheds lights on how to bring models to data using GMM and likelihood principles.

name: Managerial Economics
description: Managerial Economics as the first year MBA core course is about exposing the students to a rigorous foundation in microeconomics, game theory and industrial organization. It aims to develop students’ capacity to analyze the economic environment in which business entities operate and understand how managerial decisions can vary under different constraints that each economic environment places on a manager’s pursuit of its goals, focusing on analyzing the functioning of markets and the economic behavior of firms and other economic agents. Some motivating examples may better describe than long words and phrases.

name: Managerial Economics
description:
The macroeconomic environment and the global context provide critical parameters for companies doing business in an increasingly integrated world. Economic expansion or recession will change all business forecasts; fluctuating exchange rates will have an impact on costs, sales, risk perceptions and debt levels; the national budget or interest-rate decisions can color a company´s future; and the overall state of the economy and its future prospects are the key elements in overseas investment, production or sales decisions and strategies. The objective of this course is to give students the basic tools of analysis  to understand  the economic  situations  that surround  them, and to develop  a framework that they can use to analyze new situations or countries that they are unfamiliar with in their future professional life.

This course will focus on the macroeconomy and the policies that governments follow, and how the interaction between free economic  forces and policy affect the business  cycle and company prospects.  It will begin by analyzing the key macroeconomic indicators --GDP, inflation and unemployment  and the business  cycle--, and evaluate  how changes  in these variables  affect businesses. It will then outline the operation of fiscal and monetary policy and explore how and why policy decisions  are made, to give students  the tools to anticipate  key policy decisions  and understand their impact on the macroeconomy.

Finally,  the course  moves  from the micro and national  levels to the global level, for al look at international  trade, exchange  rates, the balance  of payments  and the processes  of economic integration. It will detail the forces of trade, the determinants of exchange rates, and the important concepts underlying the balance of payments; and how all of those elements of the international economy affect business. In the process, we will encounter an explanation for the Great Contraction that occurred beginning in 2008, and will be able to understand how the crisis will change our economic lives.

Begin with the key indicators  --GDP,  inflation and unemployment and the business cycle--,  and evaluate how changes in these variables affect business prospects. It will outline the operation of fiscal and monetary policy and how and why policy decisions are made, to give students the tools to anticipate key policy decisions and understand their impact on the macroeconomy. Finally, it will look at international trade, exchange rates, the balance of payments and the processes of economic integration to explore the costs and benefits of different situations and how they affect the business environment. In the process, we will encounter an explanation for the Great Contraction that occurred beginning in 2008, and will be able to understand how the crisis will change our economic lives.

name: Game Theory
description:
Individuals and organizations with divergent objectives and interests often compete against one another in a variety of situations. For instance, companies compete for customers and production rights, countries compete for foreign investments and over trade quotas, co-workers compete for promotions, graduates compete for jobs and contestants on game shows compete for prize money.  These agents may have identical or different strategic options open to them and may possess common information and/or private knowledge that could place them at an advantage relative to their rivals. 

This elective course provides a foundational introduction to the principles and applications of game theory. Students will learn the principles of non-cooperative and cooperative game theory, and be exposed to the application of game-theoretic models to business strategy. The concepts of Nash equilibrium, prisoners’ dilemma, game of chicken and other common forms of strategic games will be discussed in the course.

name: Managerial Microeconomics
description: This module, together with Managerial Macroeconomics, builds the foundation for all the other courses that follow.  We cover from the classical school to the contemporary developments in economic theory, putting emphasis on practical applications.  Microeconomics develops strategic thinking on how to manage a company or a corporation

name: Managerial Macroeconomics
description: Managerial Macroeconomics, by contrast to Microeconomics, focuses on managing the economy instead of an enterprise. This module helps managers understand government policies aimed at controlling inflation and unemployment, using fiscal, monetary, or other means.

name: Econometrics II
description: This course covers empirical model construction, estimation, diagnostics and selection for economic models. Problems specific to both time series and cross section data will be discussed. Topics on panel data and limited dependent variables will also be included.

name: Principles in Int'l Trade
description: This course aims to equip business students with the economic tools to analyze contemporary economic issues arising from the participation of countries in the international trading system. Some of the questions we will be asking are: why do countries trade? Why do some countries export cars, and other countries export hospital services? How has the role played by Singapore and East Asia in the global economy changed in the last few decades? Why do countries protect their economies from foreign competition? Should countries sign trade agreements with other countries, and if so, should they be multilateral or bilateral?

name: International Finance
description: This course aims to provide students with an understanding of how the global monetary and financial system works. It provides a framework for analyzing issues that arise from the participation of countries in such a global system.  Specifically, it addresses issues such as how exchange rates are determined, the linkages between domestic monetary policy and exchange rate policy, the problem of global imbalance, issues related to currency and financial crises; the evolution of global monetary system and the desirability of a common currency etc.

name: Labour, Human Capital, and Edu
description: This module examines the labor market, and which the education system best promotes human capital accumulation. There have been fundamental changes in public opinion, almost like a watershed, shifting in favor of privately funded tertiary education while pre-tertiary education remains publicly funded. We will discuss why this is so.

name: Money, Banking & Capital Flows
description: The 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis has transformed the nature of central banking, monetary policy, global banking and international capital flows profoundly. It has also led to intense debates about the appropriate roles for various institutions in maintaining a stable global financial environment. This course aims to provide an understanding of how the monetary and financial system works. It explains how policies from central banks and regulatory authorities as well as practices of commercial banks affect not only global capital flows but also the stability of the financial system and the performance of the economy. It covers issues such as the conduct of monetary policy, the operations of the commercial banks, what drives international capital flows, how banking and financial crises occur, reforms for the financial system and the role of reserve currency etc.

name: Public Finance
description:
This course introduces the public sector of a nation’s economy. Topics include the
rationales for public sector activity, fiscal accounts and analysis, fiscal (public debt)
sustainability, tax policy, and basic issues in government expenditure. A final session
will cover fiscal decentralization and fiscal rules.

name: Financial Econometrics
description: This module develops special econometric methods to study and predict movements in major financial markets in the world.

name: Inst, Indus Org, & Game Theory
longName: Institutions, Industrial Organization, and Game Theory
description: Just as game theory has made important contributions to economics, so too economists have made important contributions to game theory. One area that is particularly suited to game analysis is how to design institutions that are organically efficient, or how to regulate markets, in order to prevent market dominance by monopolist players.

name: Managing Economic Growth
description: Economic growth has emerged as top strategic policy goal for most countries in recent years. This module will introduce the contemporary growth theory, in order to examine how countries can grow faster and for longer.

name: Economics of IT
description: The impetus for economic growth in this new century is information technology. This module asks whether old economic theories remain relevant in this information age, and to what extent we need new theories to understand what some call The New Industrial Revolution.

name: Ethical Issues in Economics
description: This course introduces students to ethical economic issues and normative policies. In welfare economics for instance, how much to spend on medical services and education beg fairness and distributional questions. In law and economics, the regulation of individuals and institutions leads to ethical debates on civil liberty. In local or international disputes, economic models can offer ethical settlements. These examples are indicative rather than exhaustive of the topics can be discussed in this established and rich area of economics.

name: Real Estate & Financial Cycles
description: This course provides an introduction to real estate markets and how they interact with financial markets and the wider economy. The global economic crisis triggered by the U.S. subprime mortgage fallout highlights the critical importance of these linkages. We will start with the basic models of real estate market and go on to discuss why well-designed and well-functioning housing finance systems matter. We will then review the housing finance policy instruments that have been commonly used in various countries on both the supply and demand side. We will next consider the special challenges posed by the cyclical nature of housing markets and the proclivity for housing booms to develop into bubbles. The final topic concerns the role of government in real estate and financial cycles. Questions to be explored include whether monetary policy should target asset prices, how government regulations of land use and housing supply interact with credit markets to generate real estate cycles, and what financial supervisory structure is needed for financial stability. The course will present theory, empirical evidence and cases.

name: Env Econs, Biz and Policy
description: This course aims to help students understand the issues on environmental policies and business, and equip them with rigorous economics methods to analyze both domestic and international environmental issues. This course emphasizes the importance of market-based approach to environmental regulations. Topics covered include welfare economic foundations, environmental policy instruments, environmental valuation, environmental accounting and business.

name: Urban Economics and Policies
description: This module extends the earlier module “Public Sector and Public Policies” to a higher, more practical level. Singapore has had many examples of public policies, some successful, others more controversial. They include the banning of chewing gum, public housing, the CPF, and the electronic road pricing (ERP). We will examine and appraise such policies in this module.

name: The Chinese Economy
description: In the twenty-first century no company, or country, can afford not to have a strategy on China. This module examines the secret behind the phenomenal success of the Chinese economy, and to appraise the growing problems that the country is facing.

name: Time Series Analy &Forecasting
description: We cover selected topics in applied econometrics, specifically instrumental variable estimation and simultaneous equation models, vector autoregression models, error-correction models, panel data, and forecasting.  The emphasis is on application of these models rather than theoretical results, with hands-on work computer work with econometric software packages (Eviews).

name: Applied Econometrics
description: This module gives students the opportunity to conduct their own research project, under supervision by the faculty, to gain hands-on experience on research and modeling.

name: Critical Fiscal Issues in SG
description: Five critical fiscal issues facing Singapore will be examined in this course.  First is the peculiar nature of the Singapore economy, the origins of which will be examined in the first session, followed by analysis in the second session of why the present focus of the fiscal system is in terms of raising productivity.  Then comes a third session where the link between reserves and supply of money is spelled out.  The last session is about how the fiscal system is linked to the foreign exchange rate of Singapore.

name: Applied Mathematical Econs
description: This course uses mathematical tools to study applied economic topics. Students will come to appreciate how mathematics pushes the economic science to a high degree of analytical rigor, and why mathematics has become increasingly indispensable in economics. This course will also equip students with basic mathematical techniques that are occasionally required in their career.

name: Globalization
description: This course explores various aspects of a process bringing separate countries, cultures, and economies into an integrated whole. We will deepen our understanding on trade and competition, examining the logics of both the pro- as well as the anti-globalization camp. We will study how economic policies take on a global dimension, demonstrated vividly by how international coordination is crucial in tackling the world financial crisis of 2009. We will even examine the social and security issues of globalization, in which we may discuss economic policies targeted at economic aids, sanctions, and terrorism.

name: Special Topics in Applied Econ
description: This module develops special econometric methods to study and predict movements in major financial markets in the world.

name: Econometrics I
description: This course introduces the modeling framework and techniques of economic data. It covers the basic principles of regression models, their estimation and inference, as well as model diagnostics and selection. The emphasis is on empirical application and data analysis. The statistical package EVIEWS will be used.

name: Managerial Economics
description:
This course covers the basic Microeconomic principles that are at the heart of managerial decision-making. These principles are taught inductively starting from simple examples and practical problems.

Microeconomics is about allocating scarce resources among alternative uses. Microeconomics is also a theory of incentives, intended as the set of rules within which people behave. Policy making (what managers might be in charge of, and surely subjected to) is intended as actions changing the incentives.

In this course attention will be paid on how individuals make decisions (first aspect of Microeconomics) and how incentives are effective in obtaining the desired outcomes (second aspect of Microeconomics). These two aspects combined together provide ample learning scope for managerial decision making.

As stated, learning is via examples and problem solving. Applications concern, mostly, pricing strategies under different settings, cost optimization, negotiations and competitive bidding, governance and agency problems, corporate and social responsibility.

name: Macroeconomic Cycles & Crises
description: This course explores the nature, origins, and consequences of macroeconomic fluctuations, with emphasis on the domestic aspects of these events. Topics will include Keynesian and real business cycle models and the estimation of potential output and output gaps;  implications of business cycles for inflation and unemployment; debt-generated macroeconomic crises, including those attributable to unsustainable fiscal policy; crises resulting from financial sector difficulties; and policy responses to fluctuations and crises.

name: Pol Economy: Global & Regional
description: This course aims to provide leaders with conceptual tools and frameworks that allow systematic thinking of environment factors that allow systematic thinking of environmental factors that restructure companies, industries, competitive balance and countries. Explore current and historical events that shaped the political and business leaders of this region and discover tools used for analyzing countries, systems, trends, stakeholders, scenario developments, regional competitive impact, investment risk and potential return assessment. The objective is to assess potential shifts in stakeholder power within an industry or country, and suggest purposeful management response to these mitigating circumstances.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Statistical Inference
description:
Statistics  abounds  in  our  everyday  lives,  from  economics  to  physics,  accountancy  to  medicine,  business  to  technology,  geography  to  law,  social  science  to  politics,  a  veritable  all-embracing  giant.  No discipline does well that  disavows  it  or belittles it.  Though  many  occupations  may  not  require  specialized  statistics  degrees,  they  demand  at  least  a working application of statistics, and able competency with data crunching, statistical software and results management.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
This  course  focuses  heavily  on  running  statistical  analyses  and  applications  through  Microsoft Excel, with interpretation of results for sound decision making in practical cases, covering the basics to higher-level statistics.

By the end of this course, students will: 

(i)	know the principles and elements of basic statistics; 
(ii)	understand the need for data collection and summarize data sets into meaningful information; 
(iii)	match and execute correct statistical procedures to different data types and write sound interpretations for use in practical decision-making.

name: Social Choice & Mechanism Des
description: The course will study the foundations of collective decision making from the standpoint of a policy maker. The first part of the course will introduce the concepts of social preferences and aggregation and analyse their role in collective decision making. The second part of the course will address a fundamental feature of economic systems, namely that agents have private information which must be elicited from them by the planner via appropriate incentive schemes. This part of the course provides a brief overview of the fields of implementation and mechanism design. Applications to situations of voting, public goods provision and auctions will be considered here. The emphasis of the course will be on concepts and applications rather than on rigourous proofs.

name: Maritime Economics
description:
Maritime Transport is one of the most Globalised Industries in the world. It is also the major facilitator of World Trade. Approximately 90% of goods traded worldwide per annum in terms of volume and 85% in terms of value are carried onboard ships. 

This course aims to provide students with a thorough understanding of major economic principles and concepts through real life applications/examples and analysis of the bulk shipping markets.

name: Asian Economies
description:
Asian Economics as a course covers Asia and ASEAN economies growing and developing their trajectories in both GDP as quantitative) and development as quality of life. Issues include is economic growth as the prerequisite to finesse economic development with a quintessentially controversial challenge related to income distribution among many other issues. What economic theories and models work in commensurate to natural resources, population and demography, roles of government and market and many other parameters in reality, are important parts in the course. Case studies in Asia and ASEAN are as illuminating as they offer insights and lessons of relative success in Asian economics.

This course consists of a set of core lectures, which will introduce students to: (a) the basic economic policy tools in land, labour and capital as classically defined; and (b) the application of such theoretical knowledge to the contextual environment of Asia and ASEAN to see the touted success of the Asian growth and development model. The Asian model branded as the Asian miracle may seem contrarian to Western models. How the fusion of East-West political economy matches the new trends in globalisation induced by information communication technology (ICT), deregulation and such, in the emerging knowledge-based economy (KBE) requires some rethinking.

name: Economics & Statistics
description:
This course provides students with a foundation understanding of theories and concepts on economics and statistics and their basic application. 
The first section of the course will address market structures, demand and supply elasticity and price mechanism, micro and macroeconomics, monetary and fiscal policies and government interventions.
In the second part, the course will focus on the analysis, testing and interpretation of statistics, distributions and probability and linear regression and correlation.

name: Microeconomics I
description:
This course covers the foundations of Microeconomics, which represent the building block of Economics. The topics covered are: Consumer choice (individual and aggregate), Producer choice (individual and aggregate), Decision under uncertainty and principles of strategic interaction (Game Theory).

The course is structured in a fair formal way, typical for its level, and makes use of language and tools from Mathematics. Proofs of results will be provided when needed, so as to get the student acquainted with the rigorous thinking and systematic approach to problems that is fundamental part of the Economics.

While abstract in its nature, the course will provide results that become useful when tackling future empirical work. Therefore the foundations are lied also with the goal of forming a well round practitioner of Economics in the applied world.

name: Microeconomics II
description: This course is the second part of the Microeconomics foundation sequence. The first part of the course will provide an introduction to extensive form games of perfect and imperfect information and solution concepts that are developed for these. The second part of the course will introduce the principles of general equilibrium theory and study the fundamental theorems of welfare economics. The last part of the course will study the general equilibrium foundations of financial economics.

name: Econometrics I
description: The main purpose of this course is to provide students with the necessary econometrics tools and techniques used to analyse data sets in economics, business and finance. The focus is on understanding the methods involved, using statistical software to provide the results and then interpreting and commenting on these results. The course introduces linear and multiple regression analysis, which remains the most commonly used statistical technique in econometrics. Extensions include model specification diagnostics, nonlinear regressions, multicollinearity, heteroskedastictiy, simultaneous equations, instrumental variable estimation, binary dependent variable, and time series data analysis.

name: Econometrics II
description: The main purpose of this course is to provide students with the necessary econometrics tools and techniques used to analyse data sets in economics, business and finance. The focus is on understanding the methods involved, using statistical software to provide the results and then interpreting and commenting on these results. The course introduces linear and multiple regression analysis, which remains the most commonly used statistical technique in econometrics. Extensions include model specification diagnostics, nonlinear regressions, multicollinearity, heteroskedastictiy, simultaneous equations, instrumental variable estimation, binary dependent variable, and time series data analysis.

name: Macroeconomics I
description: This course is the first part of a two-part sequence. The aim of this sequence is to provide students with an in-depth knowledge of the macro-economy and of recent macroeconomic phenomena through the exposure to modern dynamic macroeconomic models. The first part of the sequence is dedicated to construct a dynamic general equilibrium framework that allows students to understand and analyse properties of business cycles both in closed and open economy setting. Tools for monetary and fiscal policy are introduced and the effectiveness of these tools is studied.

name: Numerical Mtds for Econ & Fin
longName: Numerical Methods for Economics and Finance
description: Computational methods comprise a collection of techniques that are practically useful in solving computational mathematics and statistics problems raised in the economics and finance field. This course would cover theories and algorithms in classic numerical mathematics, which include solving linear and nonlinear system, polynomial interpolation and numerical integration. It would also cover other numerical methods that are particularly useful in financial economics, such as random variate generation, lattice tree model and Monte Carlo simulation. The techniques discussed will be applied, using Matlab or other computational software/language, to solve computational problems in Economics and Finance (e.g., portfolio optimization, risk measurement, yield curve building, option pricing).

name: Emerging Mkt Econ & investment
description:
Over the last decade, the world has witnessed a sustained, synchronised and rapid growth phase of emerging markets, from Brazil to Turkey to China to Indonesia.  Their continued strong growth in the wake of the global financial crisis convinced many that the future belongs to emerging markets. The acronym BRIC was expanded to BRIICS, with at least another 10 countries expected to join this privileged club.  However, in the last 1-2 years, many of the former stars are losing some of the shine. China, India and Brazil are slowing down, some more rapidly than others. On the other hand, Indonesia seems to continue its strong growth, and the Philippines are surprising many on the upside. Then there is Vietnam, which went through a boom-bust cycle.

What drive economic development and growth?  Can countries succeed in doing so for decades? What are the policy choices available? How important are the soft factors relative to the hard factors? What role, if any, do conditions and policies in the developed world play? How do we know if a few years of growth spurt will not fizzle out or end disastrously? 

These are questions of relevance to policy makers as well as to senior executives contemplating sizeable, long term investments in emerging countries.  At a personal level, many executives also face the choice of having their careers ride on the success of some of these emerging markets, in a globalised world.

Important as these questions are, the economic literature available to senior executives can be superficial and confusing. Take population as an example.  In the 1970’s, rapid population growth was widely considered detrimental to economic development.  In recent years, this is touted as positive via “demographic dividends”.  Urbanisation has been rising in tandem with economic development, but the direction of causality is unclear.

name: Financial Econometrics I
description: The application of econometric methods to the characterisation of financial data, and to the estimation and testing of selected models of modern finance theory. Areas to be covered include: the statistical modelling and forecasting of financial time series, with application to share prices, exchange rates and interest rates; the specification, estimation and testing of asset pricing models including the capital asset pricing model and extensions; the modelling of volatility; practical application of volatility forecasting.

name: Financial Econometrics II
description: The application of econometric methods to the characterisation of financial data, and to the estimation and testing of selected models of modern finance theory. Areas to be covered include: the statistical modelling and forecasting of financial time series, with application to share prices, exchange rates and interest rates; the specification, estimation and testing of asset pricing models including the capital asset pricing model and extensions; the modelling of volatility; practical application of volatility forecasting.

name: Global Economics
description: This course provides a broad but rigorous look at the international aspects of economics. The course is divided into two sections: the microeconomic section with a focus on trade, and the macroeconomic section with a focus on the international finance aspects. The trade section establishes the foundations of comparative advantages and the benefits of trade and assesses the issues of international policy concerning trade, including current contentions and controversies. The second section broadens the horizons to include international payments and flows of money, the issue of surpluses and deficits and international policy concerning exchange rate and monetary regimes.

name: Economics of Competition Law
description: Antitrust, competition or anti-monopoly laws aim to prevent or discourage businesses from engaging in anticompetitive behaviour. From the enactment of the Sherman Act (1890) in the United States until the 1970s, competition laws existed only in a handful of industrialized countries. In the last few decades, however, many countries around the world have adopted competition policies and established independent competition authorities. The number of countries with competition laws has grown from around twenty in 1980 to more than a hundred by 2005. The Competition Commission of Singapore was established in 2005 while China’s first comprehensive competition law commenced in 2008. This course aims at giving students an introduction to the basic issues of competition law: market power and market definition, abuse of dominance, cartels and tacit collusion, vertical restraints, mergers and remedies.

name: Econs of Health & Healthcare
longName: The Economics of Health and Healthcare
description: This module examines current controversies in the financing and delivery of health care. As populations age and the pace of medical innovation increases, health care systems face major challenges in satisfying their populations’ rising demand for health care. This module provides students with insight into some of these challenges and an understanding of the economic tools that are necessary to develop solutions.  Topics covered will include the challenges of rationing health care, the use of cost-utility analysis, health care financing systems and health care costs.

name: Managerial Economics
description: The economic environment provides many of the critical parameters for companies doing business in an increasingly integrated world. Economic expansion or recession will change all business forecasts; market structure will affect profitability; fluctuating exchange rates will have an impact on costs, sales, risk perceptions and debt levels; and the state of the national budget or interest-rate decisions can color a company ́s future. In particular, a global recession like the one suffered recently can transform consumption behavior and business strategies. Managerial Economics provides students with a framework to understand the main economic variables and dynamics that affect business activity. Understanding the microeconomy is the first stepping-stone toward achieving a full grasp of the economic world that surrounds us. Most of the world ́s countries rely on free markets to make most of their economic decisions, and those markets automatically answer the key economic questions (What will we produce? How will we produce it? At what price? Who will get it?) through the operation of supply and demand. The course will review the basic concepts of supply, demand, market failures and externalities to provide a broad perspective on how free markets work. It will then move on to elasticity and market structures and their impact on profitability. The objective is to give students a firm understanding of how supply and demand at the micro-level determine the basic parameters of doing business. Yet markets are not perfect. In our times, a period of deregulation and strong faith in markets to solve economic problems has been followed by the deepest economic crisis since the early 20th century, with devastating effects on output, income and employment nearly everywhere. The experience has brought back to the fore the key questions of how economic decisions should be made, and how much governments should intervene when market failures exist, especially in light of pressing problems such as environmental deterioration which the market appears poorly equipped to solve. The second part of the course will focus on the macroeconomy and the policies that governments follow, and how the interaction between free economic forces and policy affect the business cycle and company prospects. It will begin by analyzing the key macroeconomic indicators --GDP, inflation and unemployment and the business cycle--, and evaluate how changes in these variables affect businesses. It will then outline the dynamics of the macroeconomy, the operation of fiscal and monetary policies and how and why policy decisions are made, to give students the tools to anticipate key policy decisions and understand their impact on the macroeconomy. Finally, the course moves from the micro and national levels to the global level, for a look at international trade, exchange rates and the balance of payments. It will detail the forces of trade, the determinants of exchange rates, and the important concepts underlying the balance of payments; and how all of those elements of the international economy affect business. In the process, we will encounter an explanation for the Great Contraction that occurred beginning in 2008, and will be able to understand how the crisis has and will change our economic lives. A special focus will be given to the Asian markets to see their dynamics.

name: Economic Analysis
description:
This is an intensive course aims to equip students with the basic knowledge and skills to understand and analyze economic issues. It is about understanding how the (economic) world works – the big picture and the fine detail – and how the actions of individuals, corporations and governments play out at the microeconomic, macroeconomic and international economic levels.

In microeconomics, we study the principles used to describe the marketplace behaviour of consumers and firms, and the characteristics of different types of product markets. Is the demand curve for a product always downward-sloping (i.e. inverse relation between price and quantity)? Where does a firm’s supply curve come from? What affects the slopes of the demand and supply curves (i.e. price
elasticities of demand and supply)? How does a firm price its product in a competitive market, in a market with a few sellers, or if the firm is the only seller in the market (i.e. monopolist)? Should firms practice price discrimination? These are some of the questions we will discuss in this section of the course.

In macroeconomics, we study the fundamental concepts of national output and income measurement, aggregate demand and supply analysis, and the analysis of the factors affecting economic growth. We discuss monetary and fiscal policies and how they are used by central banks and governments to mitigate the severity of economic fluctuations and to achieve other policy goals. What is quantitative
easing and how is it different from conventional monetary policy? Why do central banks impose negative interest rates and how does it work? Are central banks running “out of ammo” to combat the global economic slowdown? Is there a role for fiscal policy? These are among some of the current issues we will discuss in this section of the course.

In international economics, we study the economy in a global context, i.e. the flows of goods and services, physical capital, and financial capital across national borders; and discuss the role of exchange rates in international trade and how exchange rates are determined. Why do countries trade? Why do some countries export cars, and some other countries export hospital services? How did agricultural subsidies lead to “rice mountain” in Thailand, and “butter mountain” and “wine lake” in Europe? Why is the perennial debt ceiling problem in the US of concern to the rest of the world? Without its own currency, how will Greece recover from its sovereign debt crisis? These are among some of the topical issues we will explore in this section of the course.

name: Fiscal Policy & Macroecon Mgmt
description:
This course explores topical issues in macroeconomics and fiscal policy, focusing on their economic dimensions and current policy concerns. The issues are (1) business cycles, potential output, and the output gap; (2) general aspects of tax policy and
administration; (3) the economics of state-owned enterprises; (4) issues related to
economic inequality; (5) economic implications of aging, in particular pension policy and health care issues; and (6) fiscal reforms and current fiscal issues in selected countries.

name: Macroecon Acct Policy Analysis
description: This course presents the data needed to assess a national economy and shows how this information can be used to recommend policy changes to improve macroeconomic performance. The first three sessions introduce the accounts and main indicators for an economy’s real, external, fiscal, and monetary sectors. The fourth session discusses the relationships among the various accounts, introducing the concept of the flow of funds. The final session addresses how to use the information in the accounts to assess an economy and consider policy options to improve its performance.

name: Foundations in Economics
description: This is a foundation course meant for students entering into SMU’s MSc Econ and MSc Financial Econ programmes, who have not had any prior economics training. There are 2 parts to this course (microeconomics and macroeconomics). Microeconomics offers vital practical insights into how consumers maximise utility, and how firms maximise profit and compete and jointly, in doing create the foundations of market economies. Our discussions will build student’ knowledge of how households and firms make decisions, allocate scare resources, face trade-offs, in light of government regulations because of market failures due to externality, public goods, and informational problems. Macroeconomics offers vital practical insights into the behavior of the whole economy or economic system. Our discussions will build students’ knowledge of policy makers’ desire to achieve macroeconomic stabilization - stable growth, along with prices and full-employment.

name: Macroeconomic Analysis
description:
This course explores major macroeconomic topics using the general equilibrium frameworks with micro-foundations. We take a rigorous approach to address income, consumption, saving, investment, economic growth, business cycles and economic policy applications. The main objective of this course is to introduce you the workhorse models of modern macroeconomics and illustrate how they are used in conducting macroeconomic research as well as implementing government policies.

The course is rigorously structured and is conducted at a fast pace. You need to clarify any doubts at the earliest by contacting me, or through group discussions with your fellow classmates. Problem sets are an integral part of the course and it is imperative that you attempt all problems.

name: Microeconomic Analysis
description:
The course covers the foundations of Microeconomics, which constitute the fundamentals of economic analysis. The topics covered are: consumer choice (individual and aggregate), producer theory, decision making under uncertainty and principles of strategic interaction (game theory). In particular, the course will provide an introduction to normal form games, extensive form games of perfect and imperfect information and to the solution concepts that are developed for these. The last part of the course will introduce the principles of general equilibrium theory and study the fundamental theorems of welfare economics.

The course is structured in a formal manner, typical for its level, and makes use of language and tools from Mathematics. Proofs of results will be provided when needed, so as to get the student acquainted with the rigorous thinking and systematic approach that is an integral part of economic analysis. Knowledge of the mathematical tools needed by an Economist is required. A non- exhaustive list is: Calculus (continuity, differentiation, integration), Constrained and Unconstrained optimization (Kuhn-Tucker conditions), Probability theory, Linear Algebra.

name: Econometric Analysis
description:
The main purpose of this course is to provide students with the necessary econometrics tools and techniques used to analyse data sets in economics, business and finance. The focus is on understanding the methods involved, using statistical software to provide the results and then interpreting and commenting on these results. The course introduces linear and multiple regression analysis, which remains the most commonly used statistical technique in econometrics. Other topics include model specification diagnostics, nonlinear regressions, multicollinearity, heteroskedastictiy, simultaneous equations, instrumental variable estimation, binary dependent variable, and OLS in matrix form.
This course requires basic knowledge of calculus, Excel, linear algebra and statistics.

name: Applied Econometrics
description:
This is an introductory econometrics course which provides students with the tools and techniques to analyse economic and financial data. We will emphasize the use and interpretation of single-equation regression techniques in formulating and testing various economic hypotheses. In particular, we will discuss model
specification, diagnostics, multicollinearity, serial correlation, heteroskedastictiy, quantitative and qualitative variables, and cross-sectional and time series data modeling. A practical orientation will be adopted focusing on identification of appropriate techniques, execution of analysis, and sound interpretation of results. Concepts will be discussed via examples and illustrations with datasets using the software EViews on the computer. (This is a hands-on course so everyone must have a laptop).

name: Explor. Data Analy. & Visual.
description: The objective of this course is (i) to get you thinking about the role of visual techniques in the analysis of economic data, (ii) to master specific visualization tools commonly used in the analysis of economic, social, and financial data, and (iii) to help you develop the capability to create custom graphics using an open source software. Several themes run through this course, including: good vs bad practices, proper interpretation and common misinterpretations, and the difficulties and limitations of visualization techniques.

name: Machine Learning in Economics
description: This course provides an overview of Machine Learning (ML) principals. The goal of the course is to teach you the basics of the ML theory and practice of ML algorithms. The course will build upon the knowledge and skills you gained in econometrics and statistics courses. Students will learn how to interpret, design, and execute empirical projects using software and skill building in critical thinking and problem solving will also be emphasized. We will additionally explain important issues and topics that recently happened in the ML literature.

name: Panel Data Analysis
description:
This course introduce models and methods for analysing panel and longitudinal data that arise from repeated measurements taken from a cross-section of subjects. These models and data have found substantive applications in many disciplines within the social and biological sciences where the describers “panel” and “longitudinal” respectively arose. This course is primarily oriented to the applications in social science including business, economics, education and sociology. Common models include (i) one-way error components panel data models (with fixed effects, random effects, or correlated random effects); and (ii) two-way error components panel data model (with fixed effects, random effects, or correlated random effects). Panel data model with heteroskedasticity and serial correlation and tests of hypotheses with panel data will also be covered. Major inference methods such as (quasi) likelihood and GMM will be briefly introduced. A brief introduction will be given to the dynamic panel data models and spatial panel data models. Throughout, the course emphasizes on the models and their applications with computer software STATA.

Prerequisites include a good background in mathematical statistics and econometrics at the level of Greene (2003): Econometric Analysis (Prentice Hall, New Jersey).

name: Microeconometrics
description: This course aims to overview some widely used applied microeconometric tools. In particular, we will cover linear regressions, IV regressions, 2SLS, discrete response models (e.g.,probit and logit regressions), sample selection models, treatment effect models, regression discontinuity designs, and random coefficients logit models for demand estimation.

name: Data Sampling
description: This module introduces the design of sample surveys and estimation procedures, with emphasis on practical applications in survey sampling. Topics include planning of surveys, questionnaire construction, methods of data collection, fieldwork procedures, sources of errors, basic ideas of sampling, simple random sampling, stratified, systematic, cluster and quota sampling, sample size determination and cost.

name: Empirical Economics
description:
This course equips students with practical knowledge for the empirical analysis of micro data, building upon the theoretical foundations laid out in previous Econometrics courses. We cover a set of econometric tools useful for answering policy questions of interest to researchers, firms, and governments. These
include linear regression, instrumental variable, difference-in-difference, regression discontinuity design. We also develop familiarity using the software Stata for data management and analysis.

Students interested in applied microeconomics (e.g. labour, development, health, public, urban) and gaining causal insights from empirical data are encouraged to take this course. A substantial part of the course will cover preparing and analysing data using Stata, with the aim of helping students become comfortable doing empirical work.

name: Computational Macroeconomics
description:
This course equips students with powerful computational tools to be used in macroeconomic analysis. Students learn how to solve macroeconomic models using computational methods, calibrate these models, and use calibrated models to address interesting questions in macroeconomics. While students are exposed to some basic macro models throughout the course, the main objective is computer implementation of macro models, possibly with real data.

This course is part of the MPhil programme. Econ PhD students and non-Econ PhD students can enroll in this course. Econometrics 1, 2, and Macro 1 are NOT prerequisite.

name: Bayesian Econometrics
description: This course is an introduction to Bayesian econometric techniques, covering the basics of the Bayesian method, applications to the simple and multiple regression models, Bayesian computational techniques, and macroeconomic forecasting.

name: Econs of Poverty & Inequality
description: This course provides an overview of how economists understand poverty and economic inequality. Topics include definitions and data on inequality and poverty, including a discussion of various poverty and inequality measures and indices; factors explaining the causes of poverty and economic inequality; the relationship among growth, poverty, and inequality, including the role of discrimination against ethnic groups and regions; country experience with poverty and inequality, with a focus on Singapore and the United States; and strategies for addressing poverty and economic inequality.
