Commonly termed Basel II, it requires banks to move away from unvalidated human judgments to testable and verifiable empirical methods in assessing risk, especially credit risk.  Countries that cannot meet with the deadline have a few years of grace period but would eventually have to adopt this new approach.  Basel II prescribes specific definitions and parameters that banks have to use for risk measurement.  The module will cover these plus the immense challenges that they pose to banks.

name: Corporate Risk Management
description: This course examines techniques and issues in corporate credit risk analysis.  The various economic, business and financial factors that affect corporate credit quality will be discussed, as will the evaluation of a corporation’s debt servicing ability and likelihood of default.  Topics will include: business and financial risk analysis, debt covenants, seniority and security structures, parental support, structural subordination, credit scoring and credit rating models, recovery prospects, credit analysis of multi-business conglomerates, and structured finance.  Practical illustrations and case studies will be used throughout the course.  Prior knowledge of fundamental financial accounting and statement analysis will be assumed.

name: Empirical Finance
description: This course will introduce key empirical research methodologies in financial economics. It will illustrate the use of econometric methods in analyzing financial data, such as stock and bond prices, interest rates, foreign exchange rates, commodity and futures prices and option prices. Topics include tests of asset valuation models such as capital pricing model, multifactor pricing models, derivative pricing models, term structure of interest rates models and event-study analysis.

name: Client Relationship Management
description: This course explores investor psychology and the different driving forces that shape the private investor’s decision-making process. The perception and management of risk from the perspective of a private investor will also be addressed in this course.

name: Fin Planning for Individuals
description: The course specifically focuses on wealth planning for high net-worth individuals and institutions. It covers the financial planning process for individuals and institutions. Topics include personal financial planning, domestic and international estate and tax planning, and the life cycle approach for asset allocation. Participants will learn about the need be an effective bridge between their clients and the investment experts. This is carried out by a professional evaluation of the client's investment objectives, preferences, risk tolerance, and expectations.

name: Investment Advisory Process
description: This course will cover the process of client advisory including the ethical concepts in wealth management based on different culture backgrounds and different historical developments. Participants will develop sensitivity towards codes of conducts in different cultures. Participants will also strengthen personal skills in handling demanding high-net-worth individuals both in business and in social settings, and will be taught how to improve their negotiation skills with customers.

name: Wealth Planning
description:
The course focuses on wealth planning. It will begin by reviewing the global move towards greater tax transparency and the impact of this on the wealth management industry. The “real” needs of wealthy individuals and global wealth-owning families will be reviewed, as well as the tools wealth managers can use to address these needs. 

The course will also provide students with an overview of taxation and inter-generational wealth planning, including the use of onshore and offshore tax centres and the tools of wealth planning, including the use of Wills, Trusts and Foundations. Students will be provided with an understanding of multi-jurisdictional issues including tax information exchange agreements. The effects of the various initiatives by regulatory agencies to institute “tax transparency” on global wealthy families will also be discussed.  These initiatives have implications for Singapore as a financial centre. The need for corporate and individual tax planning by Singapore-based families as well as non-Singapore families will also be reviewed.

The second part of the course will consist of on-site visits to banks and financial institutions to appreciate the process of wealth planning and management in the current environment. It will complement the class seminars and issues raised.

name: Spec. Topics in Wealth Mgmt
description:
This course will cover special topics relevant to wealth management. In particular the course will deal with the landscape of wealth management in Switzerland, Family Businesses and the Family Offices.

The first part of the course discusses Family Business, a highly complex structure which has many facets and problems which can potentially lead to business failure or exit. It also analyzes successful inter-generation succession planning based on research into leading international family businesses. Case studies will illustrate the peculiarities of family business and liquidity events.

The second part of the course consists of seminars covering a wide range of topics including the current wealth management market in Switzerland, regulatory issues and emerging trends, Single Family Offices, Multi-Family Offices and investment advisory practices of Swiss private banks. There will also be visits to one or more private banks in Switzerland and networking opportunities with Swiss Bankers.

name: Advanced Study Project
description: All candidates are required to complete a project under supervision. This is a major paper which will allow candidates to apply the concepts and principles of wealth management in a commercial setting. Candidates may focus (but are not limited) their projects on one of the following areas: (1) Private banking (2) Asset management (3) Innovative products, processes or services in wealth management. For example, candidates may select a \"true-to-life\" situation, interview a number of \"clients\" to extract critical information, carrying out analysis, and propose feasible solution(s), and address the clients’ concerns and objectives. Academic and industry references will be incorporated where relevant. Products, services and processes will be analysed within the situation. Project should be designed in such a way that candidates have clear opportunity to demonstrate their: (a) technical knowledge, (b) interpersonal skills, (c) client-awareness/focus, (d) ethical standards, (e) professionalism.

name: Fin Econ : Mkt Microstructure
description:
The main objective of this seminar course is to develop a working knowledge and a suite of methods to estimate and test various models proposed in the finance literature. To dovetail with the other course on financial econometrics, this seminar course has a focus in market microstructure. The course aims to help students in developing deeper insights into the microinnards of financial economics. These insights will be useful in their future endeavours in either the industry or academics.

Some of the econometric tools that will be applied in this seminar course include the Wold representation theorem, co-integration analysis, vector autoregression (VAR), generalized method of moments (GMM), and error correction model (ECM). They should have learnt these techniques from the courses on econometrics in Term 1, or from the other related courses.

Some of the stochastic processes that they should also know include geometric Brownian motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, jump process and jump-diffusion process.

name: Finance
description: This course ams to provide students with a strong foundation in finance. Students will be exposed to key financial concepts commonly used by managers to make sound financial decisions including financial statement analysis, time value of money, investment and project analysis, risk-return analysis, and cost of capital. Lessons will also include extended discussions and analysis of the contemporary corporate scene and global capital markets.

name: Client-Centric Wealth Mgt
description: This course features topical issues on the role of a Private Banker as a client's trusted advisor.  It will discuss contemporary issues relating to the wealth management industry.  Key areas that will be covered include client relationship management, client profiling, client acquisition process and key drivers of a successful private bank.

name: Structured Products
description: This course will cover the use of structured products by fund managers for investment. These products include convertible bonds, mortgaged-backed securities, option-embedded bonds, equity-linked notes, dual currency options, reverse floaters and similar forms of innovative financial instruments. Participants will obtain a good understanding of the risk and return of these products, and their use in portfolio management.

name: Investments
description: This course focuses on empirical tests of asset pricing models, option pricing models and recent empirical evidence on asset pricing, option pricing and investment.  The topics covered include empirical tests of market efficiency, consumption-based asset pricing models, Black-Scholes and stochastic volatility option pricing models, and cross-section determinant of stock returns.  Although emphasis will be on the empirical works, some related theories will also be discussed.

name: Corporate Gov. - Fin. Pers.
description:
The course surveys leading academic research in the area of corporate governance, placing emphasis on boards of directors, institutional investors and the influence of corporate and securities law upon corporate finance.

Recent working papers will be studied to familiarise students with latest developments in the field. Topics covered include the importance of governance, agency costs and organisational form, theories of boards, the directors, boards and firm value, governance and mergers & acquisitions, governance and corporate restructuring, institutional investors etc.

name: Analy of Derivative Securities
description:
Financial derivatives have applications across many areas of finance, such as hedging, swaps, convertible claims, and corporate decision making. The course objective is for students to understand profoundly the valuation of forward, futures, options and other derivative securities, and their use in hedging risk exposures, such as commodity price risk, currency risk, interest rate risk, stock portfolio risk, and so forth.

Good intuition is more important than math for understanding derivative concepts. In my teaching (including the assignments and exams), I will minimize the use of math but focus on the economic intuition.  

In addition, students will be given the opportunity of using a comprehensive online financial markets simulation system called Stock-Trak to obtain hands-on experience (of a hedge fund manager) in trading in the “real” market. For instance, students can trade futures and options on commodities such as gold, silver, corn, oil etc at the ‘market prices’ through Stock-Trak.

name: Advanced Corporate Finance
description: The objective of this course is to help students develop further understanding of current theories and their implications for solving financial problems. The approach taken is that of financial strategy. The major topics covered include wealth creation and the enhancement of shareholder value, managing working capital and corporate growth, corporate capital investments, capital structure and corporate payout policy, real options, investment banking and capital raising, mergers and acquisitions, etc. Throughout the course, we will study the problems which corporations face in making investment decisions with an emphasis on valuation. Research results from recent empirical work and their implications for corporations will also be discussed, where appropriate. Cases will be used to illustrate the concepts and tools introduced in the course.

name: Equity Analy & Portfolio Mgmt
description: This module covers basic techniques of valuation and management of securities in a portfolio context. For valuation of stocks, models such as discounted cash flow models, P/E multiples, and alternative-pricing models will be covered. Implication of efficient market theory on fundamental and technical analysis will also be examined.  Global and local equity market features will be incorporated to add depth to the module. For portfolio management, concepts of risk and return are analyzed in the context of formal pricing models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model and the Arbitrage Pricing Theory. Aspects of efficient market theory and anomalies are considered. The concept of portfolio diversification and the construction of optimal portfolios such as mean-variance efficient portfolios are studied. The syllabus extends to the consideration of international diversification and investments where currency risks and interest rate risks need to be evaluated.

name: Equity Analy & Portfolio Mgmt
description: This course would cover the current theories of portfolio management and provide a conceptual framework for the evaluation of investment strategies. It aims to provide students with exposure to the process of investment management including identification of investment objectives and constraints, determining asset allocations, and measuring portfolio performance. It will also cover the fundamental concepts of investments, including risk and return, market efficiency, portfolio diversification, CAPM and risk management using derivatives. Lessons will also include extended and interactive discussions and analyses of the contemporary investing scene and global capital markets.

name: Financial Modeling
description: Managers very often need to make important quick decisions.  These are usually difficult to justify without a good model and thorough analysis.  This course focuses on helping students learn to use spreadsheets as effective tools in financial modeling.  Through practices in class, students will be able to develop on their own spreadsheet models, covering representative topics from corporate finance to investments planning and analysis, to analyze trade-offs and sensitivities, and understand implications of uncertainties and risks.  The key emphasis of this course is on acquiring the necessary programming skills and developing the art of modeling, more than learning about available financial models.

name: Financial Modeling
description: Managers very often need to make important quick decisions.  These are usually difficult to justify without a good model and thorough analysis.  This course focuses on helping students learn to use spreadsheets as effective tools in financial modeling.  Through practices in class, students will be able to develop on their own spreadsheet models, covering representative topics from corporate finance to investments planning and analysis, to analyze trade-offs and sensitivities, and understand implications of uncertainties and risks.  The key emphasis of this course is on acquiring the necessary programming skills and developing the art of modeling, more than learning about available financial models.

name: Managerial Finance
Global Financial Markets
description: This course will focus on the practical operations and institutional aspects of domestic and international financial institutions, including commercial and investment banks. Topics include stocks, bonds, options and futures markets. Capital market activities and their processes, including initial public offers, mergers and acquisitions and capital bankruptcy will be also discussed.

name: Alternative Investments
description: Basic overview of alternative investments with focus on hedge funds, private equity, real estate and commodity investment. The course is suited for those who are interested to have a basic understanding of the alternative investments industry. Real life examples and case studies would be use widely and this course will be taught by current practicing practitioners. Topics on due diligence processes, general investment terms and structure, valuation approaches, and exit/divestment strategies will be discussed.  Fundamental investment principles such as discounted cash flow models, EV/EBITDA multiples, and alternative-pricing models will be covered. A case study as an example of a practical, hands-on, problem solving approach to commercial real estate investment will be discussed.

name: Alternative Investments
description: This course provides both a theoretical and practical look into the world of managing Alternative investments and their role in a multi-asset class portfolio.

name: Corporate Finance
description: Although corporate finance is traditionally a finance topic, we will introduce it from an economist’s perspective. The purpose of this module is to understand how corporations, or how any company, make strategic finance decisions. Such decisions include long term planning, short term inventories, and borrowing and lending.

name: Corporate Finance
description: This course aims to provide students with an advanced study of Corporate Finance beyond the essentials.  Students will be exposed to complex financial concepts and be equipped with the necessary analytical tools to make routine and strategic financial decisions.  The course covers a wide spectrum of topics such as appraisal of cross-border investment projects, optimal capital structure, initial public offerings, rights issue, mergers & acquisitions, value creation, corporate restructuring and risk management.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Corporate Finance
description:
The course will provide an occasion to understand that finance is concerned with:

• Forecasting availability or scarcity of money rather than keeping internal historical records of where it has come from or where it is going to.

• Dealing with the uncertainty and risk that surrounds future developments rather than with the accuracy of information in recording the monetary impact of past and current operations.

• Focusing on value creation for shareholders rather than on fairly allocating responsibility for money among the different parts of a company.

• Becoming aware of the limitations in understanding and using financial models, so that we can avoid using tools that we do not fully understand just because their use provides high personal incentives in the short run, at the expense of many others in the longer run.

name: Behavioral Finance
description: The course introduces students to the core questions asked by behavioral scientists and behavioral finance researchers via a collection of seminal articles and demonstrations (both in-class and outside-class). It is an inter-disciplinary course which spans topics in finance, psychology, and decision science. We will first discuss conventional finance paradigm and its empirical challenges. We then proceed with four weeks of in-depth discussions of behavioral foundations, followed by another four weeks of application topics related to financial markets and investments.

name: Research Seminar in Finance
description: This course will focus on the “state of the art” empirical research in finance.  The topics will cover areas such as empirical asset pricing, corporate finance and corporate governance.   Students will be reading both published and “working papers” on these topics and will attend seminars and research workshops on these topics.  In the conclusion of the course, students will be expected to write an original research paper in one of these topics.

name: Mergers and Acquisitions
description:
The Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A) market is widely regarded as a market for corporate control, where  firms  are  acquired  or  merged  for  a  variety  of  right  or  wrong  reasons. Some  M&A transactions  are  pursued  for  strategic  reasons  –  to  improve  the  effectiveness  and  efficiency (synergistic) of the underlying business. M&A transactions could also be undertaken by management to pursue their own interests, such as managerial entrenchment, which would be value destroying to the shareholders. In the latter case, the market could intervene by punishing the management via the takeover market.

This course serves to familiarize participants with the nuances of the M&A market.   Specifically, it aims to explain the role that M&A play in corporate strategy development.  In this respect, some of the related questions will be explored: Why firms undertake these transactions?  What is the genesis of  value  in  these  transactions? How  much  value, if  any, is created? Who  gains  from  these transactions? What is the track record of value creation for M&A deals? How does M&A market relate to corporate restructuring?

An important focus is relating the theory to the practical aspect of a deal. Here, participants will be exposed to valuation techniques and issues; structuring considerations; aspects of M&A execution including negotiation strategies, due diligence, documentations, legal and regulatory issues. Post- acquisition integration which is a crucial part of M&A transactions will also be discussed.

This course will be relevant for those planning to pursue a career in finance or general management in a corporate setting as well as those planning to pursue a career in private equity or at a deal intermediary, such as an investment  bank.   As such, there will be some discussions on how an investment bank organizes its corporate finance department  and how this product fits with other parts of its capital raising business.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Global Financial Markets
Hedge Funds & Related Alt. Inv
longName: Hedge Funds and Related Alternative Investments
description:
This course will explore issues related to hedge funds from the perspectives of traders, potential investors and financing counterparties of such strategies.  The emphasis is for the students to be as hands-on as feasible, in terms of taking trading strategies from inception to execution.  The goal of the course is to teach students to analyze hedge fund strategies at the trade level and at the portfolio level, and to understand the potential implications of hedge fund activities to the global financial economy.

The materials will be based on those developed for an investment management course jointly by SMU with Stanford GSB.

name: Private Equity & Venture Cap.
description:
The level of entrepreneurial activity in an economy is an important determinant of its long-term growth potential.  Besides the availability of a large talent pool and a conducive business environment, the access to venture capital and other types of entrepreneurial financing is a crucial factor in stimulating high-growth entrepreneurial activity.  

This elective course explores topics and issues in private equity and venture capital investing. We will cover the principles of entrepreneurial financing, from the perspective of an entrepreneur looking to build his venture, as well as from the perspective of venture capitalist looking to invest in promising startups.   

Investment principles as well as valuation models such as discounted cash flow models, P/E multiples, and alternative-pricing models will be covered.  The different types of valuation models such as discounted cash flow models, P/E multiples, and alternative-pricing models will be discussed.  We will also discuss the different forms of exit strategies, including initial public offering, trade sales and buyouts.

name: The Theory & Policy of Mod Fin
longName: The Theory and Policy of Modern Finance
description:
This course emphasizes problem solving and applications for the theories of modern finance. What efficiencies of markets means in a practical sense is demonstrated, the economic model of the firm is compared with the accounting model, the weaknesses of the accounting framework are demonstrated in valuation of acquisitions and designing incentive contracts for management. Dividend policy and capital structure are investigated as they relate to changes in share value and the price-to-earnings ratio. The concept of cost of capital is shown to be independent of capital structure even in the real world, a principal component of the Miller-Modigliani theorems in a world of perfect capital markets. Finally,
three alternate models are presented for pricing firms, including initial public offerings, acquisitions and divestitures and for internal capital allocation. Strategic planning and valuation is reconciled and the EVA framework is used for designing incentive contracts for management, boards of directors and even for all employees right down to the shop floor. The emphasis is on real world illustrations. The student should have achieved a practical understanding of the theories of modern finance when the course is completed.

name: Analy. & Appln of Derivatives
description: This course covers options, forward contracts, futures contracts and swaps.  Participants will discuss how these instruments work, how they are used, and how they are priced including basic valuation models such as the Black-Scholes model.  It will discuss the application of some mathematical concepts to better understand derivatives from a practical perspective with key focus on the intuition.  The course will discuss the pricing of derivatives, opportunities and risks involved in trading derivatives.  Many securities have embedded derivatives and these can range from the simple to the complex in structured products.  This course will lay the groundwork for the next course, Structured Products.

name: Finance (Introductory Section)
description:
This course material is the Introductory Section from the complete Finance Online Course. Courses may be adopted in their entirety or by individual sections.

The Introductory section of the Finance presents the fundamental ratios and forecasting methods used to make business decisions. Course topics include: Financial Statements / Ratio Analysis / Growth / Profitability / Efficiency / Liquidity / Leverage / Risk / Common-Size Financial Statements / Interpretation / List of Common Ratios / Qualifications / Cash Cycle and Growth / Cash Cycle / Sources and Uses / Growth / Financial Forecasting / Basic Ingredients / The Process / Bias, Error and Uncertainty / Pro Formas / Time Value of Money and Project Valuation / Compounding and Discounting / Investment Decision Criteria / Perpetuities.

Seat time for the section is 7 to 9 hours, depending on the student's experience with the material.

name: Research Methods in Finance
description: This course aims to provide students with a strong foundation in using the SAS software to conduct empirical research in finance. SAS programming solutions and strategies to typical finance research questions will be discussed in detail and potential pitfalls will be outlined. Throughout the course, students will be required to read and familiarize themselves with classical and recent empirical papers in the area of empirical finance. Substantial time will be devoted to conducting data analysis with the SAS software and understanding various approaches to solve issues (such as heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation) which are related to financial econometrics.

name: Theory of Finance
description: This course will examine the foundations of modern finance theory, with emphasis on asset pricing and portfolio choice. The first half of the course will focus on the underlying theory of financial economics, with topics such as decision making under uncertainty, linear valuation and factor models, and single and multi-period portfolio choice. The second half of the course will focus on recent developments as well as areas of current research, with topics such as asset pricing anomalies, time- and state-inseparable preferences, and behavioral finance.

name: Research Seminar in Finance II
description: This course will focus on the \"state of the art\" empirical research in finance. Students will be reading both published and \"working papers\" on topics in finance and will attend seminars and research workshops on these topics. In the conclusion of the course, students will be expected to write an original research paper in one of these topics.

name: China Economy & its Finan Mkts
longName: China Economy and its Financial Markets
description:
This series of lectures addresses emerging issues of China economy, plus operations and consequences of China financial markets. China economy has transformed from totally state-owned economy to capitalism that requires strong support from financial markets. Fortunately, China owns Hong Kong which can provide benchmark of capitalism development of China. To watch development of China financial markets could partly understand consequences of China economy.
In 2011, China stock market resulted the worst performance in the world, although economic growth in China is greater than 10%. In addition, you can also find average offered price of Chinex (創業板) has long been greater than 50 times of P/E ratio (Price/Earnings ratio) since its first IPO; its highest one was ever 122 times. Also, 100 times P/E ratio or of above in secondary trading market can be easily found both in A share and Chinex markets. China recently has suffered inflation, RMB currency controversy, substantial amount of local governmental debts in China, and others, Asset bubble may slow down economic growth of China economy. Many interesting issues of China economy and its financial markets can be explored.

name: Hedge Funds
description: This course serves as an introduction to the secretive and fascinating world of hedge funds. The aim is to provide students with an understanding of the various hedge fund strategies and the risks that they are exposed to. By understanding the investment issues, agency problems, and operational constraints that hedge funds grapple with, students will be equipped with the skills to select hedge fund products. The course will be useful for aspiring chief investment officers, asset managers, private bankers, family office managers, prime brokers at investment banks, hedge fund managers, and hedge fund investors.

name: Portfolio Analysis
description: This short course focuses on the concepts, analytical tools and process of portfolio management. It will cover the basic concepts of investments, including risk and return, portfolio diversification and performance evaluation. Seminars will also include case studies and the development of appropriate investment policy statements for individuals and institutions. Students will be participating in a simulated investment activity.

name: Financing Decisions
description: This course equips participants with the conceptual and analytical foundations for corporate financial decisions involving capital structure, financing choices, cost of capital, and dividend policy. It also discusses the market for corporate finance and control, including IPOs, seasoned debt and equity offerings, bank loan market, venture capital, mergers and acquisitions, and corporate restructuring.

name: Business Valuation
description: This course provides participants with an in-depth understanding of valuation models used to evaluate investment decisions and determine asset values. Participants will learn techniques used to forecast cash flows and estimate cost of capital and growth rates.

name: Corporate Finance
description: This course aims to provide students with a broad overview of Corporate Finance.  It addresses three financial decisions faced by business firms: (a) How to invest? (b) How to finance and (c) How to operate profitably? The course will equip students with conceptual and analytical skills necessary to make both routine and strategic financial decisions. It will cover return and risk concepts, capital budgeting, cost of capital, capital structure, Mergers & Acquisitions and Value Creation. Cases will be used to illustrate the concepts and tools introduced in the course.

name: Advanced Corporate Banking
description: This course is structured to provide participants with advanced knowledge of credit analysis and corporate relationship management principles and techniques that are applicable to corporate lending decisions in financial institutions. The loan portfolio is generally the major asset category on a commercial bank’s balance sheet and the revenues generated from corporate lending activities account for more than half the net interest income generated by most universal banks. Hence, the establishment and management of the corporate loan asset require the understanding and application of appropriate techniques to achieve good loan quality, control, monitoring and management of credit risk factors to achieve loan repayment. Given the severe negative impact of the most recent global financial crisis, a good understanding of the nature, scope and impact of credit risk in the financial industry and economy at large is of paramount importance. The course aims to equip graduate students with an advanced knowledge base in making good corporate lending decisions as a corporate banker and for those who are interested in pursuing a corporate banking career in the banking industry.

name: Empirical Finance I
description: This course is aimed to help students to obtain an in-depth understanding of the major empirical finance issues, particularly in investments. This course would also cover the current theories of portfolio management and provide a conceptual framework for the evaluation of investment strategies. It aims to provide students with exposure to the process of investment management including identification of investment objectives and constraints, determining asset allocations, and measuring portfolio performance. Topics include models of stock returns, multifactor asset pricing models, asset allocation, stock screening, predictability, performance evaluation, anomalies, and limits to arbitrage. It will also cover the fundamental concepts of investments, including risk and return, market efficiency, portfolio diversification, and risk management. Based on recent research articles and cases, students are required to learn the empirical facts, theories and the associated statistical tools to analyze financial data. The coverage will include applications and implementation.

name: Mathematics of Fixed Income
description: This is a course on the mathematics of interest rates and bond management. Students will go through the basic theories of interest rates, including the computation of the future and present values of annuities. There will be an introduction to bond investments and the risks involved, including pricing formulas, measurement of returns, interest-rate risk, interest-rate swaps, reinvestment risk and other risks. Estimation and theory of term structure will be discussed. Techniques for using bonds to immunize interest-rate risks, including target-date immunization, duration matching and Redington immunization will be covered.

name: Research Sem in Finance III
description: This course aims to reinforce student’s understanding of high quality research in finance, both in the empirical asset pricing and corporate finance area. Students will be reading yet to be published empirical research working papers.  Substantial time will be spent studying issues in both asset pricing and corporate finance and how one can use financial econometric tools to investigate these issues. In the conclusion of the course, students will be able to critique a piece of research in detail.

name: Corporate Finance
Fin Mgmt & New Venture Fin
longName: Financial Management and New Venture Financing
description:
Through the internalisation of knowledge about Finance and Best Practices, this course aims at making students more skilful and confident (i) in making decisions, (ii) in the search for partners, and (iii) in negotiations regarding the financial resources which enable innovation. Four topics, which are of highest importance for innovative activities, will be highlighted throughout the course:
 
1. Financing firms in transition – the Importance of Accountability and of Safeguards. 
2. Risk from inside and from outside – Identification and Management. 
3. Real options – their Creation, Maintenance, and Valuation.
4. Exit strategies and capital market transactions – ways of bringing innovation into forms which investors recognize.

name: Cases in Corporate Finance
description: FNCE 675 is a comprehensive course in corporate finance that builds directly on techniques learned in FNCE 650 (which is a pre-requisite). The course is designed to emphasize teamwork, which is required for producing written analytical reports and attaining successful negotiated outcomes. The course focuses on Market Value Balance Sheet (MVBS) analyses of specific problems and cases in financial economics. In particular, the students will learn to value and analyze intra-corporate and inter-corporate transactions, including advanced financial instruments in the context of corporate control contests, and understand related legal issues. There will be 3 case analyses and negotiations that are strictly team exercises. Depending on the specific topic, each team will be assigned a different “role” of the same case (e.g., a company engaging an investment banker; a company seeking to acquire another company; etc.). Each team will provide a written report for the case and conduct negotiations with other teams (depending on the perspective assigned) to close a deal on the corresponding transaction.

name: Investment Banking
description: This course aims to provide insightful perspective into the investment banking industry that covers financing for corporations through the capital markets in the form of equity, debt and variations along the capital structure, advising on mergers & acquisitions (M&A) on both the buy-side and sell-side, and managing risk to address a corporation’s most critical financial and strategic challenges. The course will also cover the history, strategy, culture and products of investment banking, the structure of investment banks and how the various departments in an investment bank inter-relate and interact, the importance of management and compliance, a discussion of who’s who of investment banking and applications of valuation and financial modeling. This course applies practical applications to financial theories and is intended for prospective investment banking candidates and also for those who are keen to learn about the investment banking industry.

name: Strategies for Wealth Mgmt
description:
Participants will develop an appreciation of Asian families and how to assist families manage their wealth employing entrepreneurial approaches and strategies which is predominantly invested in diverse businesses. This course will explore strategic approaches that are vital to family wealth management, such as effective approaches to structuring a family company, succession planning, conflict resolution and wealth education for the next generation, with a view to staging companies for leadership, management and growth. 

Of high interest to all participants will be the sections on the formulating and implementation of a strategy by wealth managers to look after the wealth of families and to extending the effectiveness of you wealth management practice.

name: Empirical Finance II
description: This course is aimed to help students to obtain an in-depth understanding of the major empirical finance issues, particularly in investments. This course would also cover the current theories of portfolio management and provide a conceptual framework for the evaluation of investment strategies. It aims to provide students with exposure to the process of investment management including identification of investment objectives and constraints, determining asset allocations, and measuring portfolio performance. Topics include models of stock returns, multifactor asset pricing models, asset allocation, stock screening, predictability, performance evaluation, anomalies, and limits to arbitrage. It will also cover the fundamental concepts of investments, including risk and return, market efficiency, portfolio diversification, and risk management. Based on recent research articles and cases, students are required to learn the empirical facts, theories and the associated statistical tools to analyze financial data. The coverage will include applications and implementation.

name: Fin &Securities Regulation
description:
This course aims to give students a practical overview of the principles and statutory regime relating to the regulation of different industries. This modules will be taught by practitioners using cases sharing their experiences and possible financial regulatory issues in different industries as an entrepreneur in different.

The first half module (3 sessions or 0.25 CU) will cover aspect of the fund management industry from the prism of a practitioner. The students will find themselves in the middle of multiparty negotiations for a multinational merger/acquisition deal. The students have to use their knowledge of quantitative analysis and modeling to evaluate different aspects of the deal, and the future problems and issues that can arise out of such deals as an analyst.

The second half module (3 sessions or 0.25 CU) will put the students in the drivers’ seat in the hedge fund industry with significant regulatory hurdles and peculiarities compared to other fund management industries. The module will cover aspects of due diligence, compliance, investment opportunities, accounting and computational issues related to the mechanics of the hedge fund industry.

name: Corporate Finance
description:
In modern day corporations, manager make decisions on behalf of provider of capital. Given the resources that have been entrusted to them, management of these corporations have an overarching objective of maximizing firm value by making the right decisions. In this course, you will be the types of decisions in corporate finance, namely investment, financing, and dividends decisions. 

The course aims to provide students with fundamentally important ideas about what to look for in making good and informed investment, financing, and dividends decisions.  Our analysis of these decisions will focus on how the right decisions can lead to the enhancement of firm value.

Students will be exposed to the concepts of risks and returns, of options value and applications in corporate finance, and of how to balance off the risks versus returns in asset pricing models will be discussed.  This tradeoff is equivalent to finding optimal value or valuation of the opportunities that present themselves to corporate business.

This course is primarily designed for participants with little or no background in finance. That said, the depth and range of concepts will be varied accordingly to ensure that even participants with grounding in finance will challenged.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Alternative Investing
description: In this course, participants will learn about alternative investments. These investments include real estate, venture capital/private equity funds, commodities and about behavioral finance. The risk and return characteristics and the market features of these different alternative asset classes will be discussed.

name: Tax, Trusts & Wealth Planning
description: This course will examine taxation and trusts in wealth management. It covers concepts of tax, tax treaties, double taxation relief, tax incentives, and how holding companies can be utilised in international tax planning. It examines the role of private trusts as instruments of dynasty planning and wealth distribution, with particular reference to issues of continuing control over gifted assets.

name: Cont. Banking in the Fin Mkts
longName: Contemporary Banking in the Financial Markets
description: Much is taught on banking in the context of economics. A typical MBA beginning in an entry-level position in a bank is told by experienced co-workers to “forget everything you learned in University.” To prepare students for what they are likely to experience upon entering the financial sector, this seminar covers the practical elements of contemporary banking, focusing on the businesses of dealing in the capital markets. Course content is designed and delivered by a former financial derivatives dealer, who has been a consultant to banks in Asia for over 12 years.

name: Derivative Securities
description: The course is intended to provide students with an understanding of forward contracts, futures contracts, options, and swaps. Derivatives on stocks, indices, foreign currency, interest rates and bonds are to be covered.

name: Derivative Securities
description:
Financial derivatives have applications across many areas of finance, such as hedging, swaps, convertible claims, and corporate decision making. The course objective is to provide students with the necessary tools and techniques to determine the fair valuation of forward, futures, options and other derivative securities, and apply derivative securities in hedging risk exposures, such as commodity price risk, currency risk, interest rate risk, stock portfolio risk, and so forth. 

Furthermore, students will be given the opportunity to explore a comprehensive online financial markets simulation system (Stock-Trak) to obtain hands-on experience (of a fund manager :) in trading in the “real” market. For instance, students can trade futures and options on commodities such as gold, silver, corn, oil etc at the ‘market prices’ through Stock-Trak. 

By taking this course, students are expected to be able to: calculate the theoretical fair prices of derivative securities (e.g. Black-Scholes Formula), utilize derivative securities in various applications, such as hedging risk exposures, timing the market, etc.

name: Financial Risk Management
description: This course offers a deep dive into Financial Risk Management, emphasizing credit and market risks—the two pivotal domains within the financial sector. By integrating foundational principles of financial risk with practical financial applications, it provides a comprehensive learning experience that bridges academic rigor with practical skills. Beginning with the fundamentals of financial instruments, risk, and return, the course progresses to advanced strategies in measuring, managing, and modeling financial risks. Through a combination of risk frameworks and practitioner-friendly implementations, participants will explore key concepts in financial risk management, including credit scoring, portfolio management, Value at Risk (VaR), and market risk models. The course strives to develop a good personal comprehension of, and a calculated inclination towards, financial risk, extending to broader contexts. This foundational insight aims to refine participants’ proficiency in making informed, risk-conscious decisions applicable to diverse real-world scenarios.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Applied Finance Research Proj
description: This supervised research project allows candidates to apply the concepts and principles of selected area(s) of finance to a commercial setting. Candidates may concentrate their research in any area of finance that has a practical focus. The research must include a survey of the relevant literature, in-depth analysis, empirical tests (where appropriate), and recommendations for their practical or policy implementation. Candidates offering this research project must have successfully completed all the required core courses of their program.

name: Trusts & Inter-Gen Wealth Plan
description: This course will introduce the concept of trusts and their role in inter-generation succession planning. It examines the role of private trusts as instruments of dynasty planning and wealth distribution, with particular reference to issues of continuing control over gifted assets.

name: Client Relationship Management
description: This course discusses the building blocks of great client experience, how to go about building a great client book and the investment advisory process.

name: International Financial Mgmt
description:
This course is intended to provide students with the necessary foundation in economics to understand the material in financial publications such as the Economist and Financial Times. The course then investigates the risks and rewards of international investing in the context of portfolio theory (asset pricing) as well as within an individual firm (corporate finance). These finance applications are the pillars of the course.

This course extends the concepts taught in introductory finance. The use of derivative securities such as futures, options, and swaps to manage risk is covered extensively. However, while knowledge of option pricing theory is beneficial, it is not required for the course.

name: Monetary Pol in Global Context
longName: Monetary Policy in a Global Context
description: This module provides students with the understanding of the operation of monetary policy, exploring the special role that money plays in a modern economy, and emphasising the myriad of different definitions of money supply. Students will also explore the crucial role that banks play in the creation of money and credit, at the same time understanding the different roles that central banks play in different economies across Asia, Europe, and the US, and consider the tools that they have to help them in reaching their objectives.

name: Corporate Finance
Financing Entrepreneurial Bus.
description: This course provides participants with an overview of the various sources of capital companies tap into in the various stages of their lifecycle. It starts with the establishment of a framework that links a company’s financing choices and capital structure to the intrinsic value of its shareholders’ equity. The bulk of the course covers the entire gambit of financing options across the lifestyle of a firm including startup funding, private equity, IPOs, and debt financing.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Fin Engrg: Intro to Derivative
description:
Financial engineering is the process of creating new financial instruments through the use of bonds, stocks and individual derivatives such as forwards, futures, swaps and options as basic building blocks. The process involves designing, pricing and managing the risks of these instruments. 

The course closes the gap between theory and practices as it constantly links risk management tools with the business that is aimed to be achieved. It starts with a quick introduction on stock markets’ fundamentals. It then uses a top-down approach that gives the readers a great idea of the world of financial derivatives segmented by solutions providers and the different types of clients and their needs in terms of hedging and yield enhancement structures. 

Once the reader understands the investors’ point of view, the appropriate solutions are introduced in a sequence of increasing complexity. Their payoffs are well explained and accompanied by real life examples. Then the course goes deeper into further details explaining pricing and risk management tools, using an intuitive approach that creates a good balance between the philosophy behind existing models and the mathematics involved.

In this course, we also anatomize a few popular structured products traded in the market. We study the risk exposure of the retail investors and risk management for the commercial banks. We also discuss some topics on the market for the volatility trading and recent development of option-pricing models.

name: Corporate Treasury Management
description:
Cash is king and treasury lies at the heart of a corporation. The receipt and payment of cash and the timing of it is critical to the solvency and profitability of the firm. The multinational firm has to hedge and convert cash in a variety of currencies. Corporate growth requires funding that is sourced from banks, bond and equity markets, and even venture capital, private equity and mezzanine financing. Corporations with surplus cash may need to place these cash or invest them for higher yields. 

Foreign exchange and interest rate and financial markets risk management is ever more important given the changing and volatile landscape of global developments. Poor risk management has caused firms to falter; some of these cases will be highlighted. In the corporate treasury, finance & banking, investment and cash management comes alive. IT enabled treasuries has front-end market access system linked to Corporate Treasury Management System with straight-through-processing into payments and accounting systems. 

This course will also feature a series of invited speakers, in which CFOs, corporate treasurers and bankers will share perspective and experience on the various topics followed by Q&A.

name: Sustainable & Impact Investing
description: This finance elective provides a thorough grounding in the conceptual and practical aspects of the discipline of portfolio management, drawing on real-life examples from the world of institutional asset management, sell-side and buy-side investment analysis, and private wealth management. The course starts with an overview of the principal players in the asset management industry and how their particular objectives impact the practice of portfolio management. Next, students receive a hands-on introduction to the essential concepts of modern portfolio theory, covering the topics of risk and return, diversification, asset allocation and systematic portfolio construction. The course then zooms in on the two most prominent asset classes of equities and fixed income, covering the essentials of individual security analysis as well as portfolio management within these two traditional asset classes. Alternative asset classes are covered in separate sessions on hedge funds and private equity/venture capital. After an introduction to the topic of performance evaluation and manager selection, the course concludes with a session on the particular context of private wealth management. Throughout the course, special attention will be given to the asset management industry landscape in Asia.

name: Entrepreneurial Finance
description:
Any successful business progresses through a life cycle – from a start-up all the way to being a successful and mature firm.  Growth firms often find financing one of the biggest hindrances to survival and growth.  As such, an entrepreneur will often be confronted with the challenges of financing the firm to achieve growth and profitability objectives.  Each financing choice have their own pros and cons, that may create additional opportunities or risks for the business venture.

Hence, understanding the choices available at each stage of the life cycle will be critical for the entrepreneur to chart the firm’s future.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Valuation & Financial Modeling
description:
The course is aimed at providing participants with a comprehensive knowledge on various valuation techniques. It focuses on tools that are used to value a variety of business propositions from a varied perspective. The course will cover ways to estimate the value of different types of users who will deploy these techniques for their intended purposes. These include investors (small and large; short
and long term; individual and institutional; insider and outsider), analysts (buy and sell side), accountants, and regulators/government agencies. In addition to the foundation afforded by the basic techniques that will apply to, the course will explore techniques in the valuation of publicly traded (small and large; in developed and emerging economies; in manufacturing, technology, and
service sectors), across their life-cycle (Start-up/Young, IPO, Mature, Declining). Students will also learn how to operationalize the concepts in valuation via financial modelling on excel spreadsheets. Students will also learn how the industry best practices with respect to financial modelling.

name: Intro to Hedge Fund & Quan Str
longName: Introduction to Hedge Funds and Quantitative Strategies
description:
The aim of this course is firstly to provide students with a broad overview of the hedge fund industry. This will include industry participants, hedge fund structure, key personnel roles and hedge fund types (strategies). Particular attention will be paid to understanding risks associated with hedge funds including business risk, credit risk, counterparty risk, liquidity risk, market risk, operational risk and personnel risk. This component of the course will include detailed discussion of the due diligence guidelines of the Alternative Investment Mangers’ Association, hence the focus is on a practical understanding of the day-to-day risks and key issues faced by hedge fund managers. Investor monitoring and selection of hedge funds for investment purposes will also be discussed.

Secondly, the course also provides an introduction to systematic investing strategies that may be employed by hedge funds. An overview of strategy types is provided, after which the students will be provided with (and are expected to be able to discuss) a range of practical examples of systematic strategy tools and techniques, including strategy implementation.

Case study discussions are employed to provide practical examples of key issues introduced in this course.

It is intended that one or more guest speakers from the industry will present their personal experiences to provide students with a perspective on opportunities and advancement within hedge funds and related financial institutions.

This course places substantial emphasis on active student participation. Classes should be viewed as discussion seminars, NOT instructor lectures. It is expected that students will have read assigned material prior to the class, and ALL students are expected to be able to discuss key issues with the instructor during classes.

name: Financial Markets
description: This course focuses on the role of financial markets in facilitating the flow of funds to finance investments by corporations and governments. We will systematically examine each market and describe the participants and types of instruments offered. The key markets examined are equity markets, debt markets, foreign exchange markets, derivative markets, real estate markets, and insurance markets. We will also examine the role of financial institutions such as commercial banks and mutual funds. This course builds on the foundations provided by FNCE680 Corporate Finance & Financial Management. Our focus will be to understand how financial markets work practically. We will also learn how and whether one should invest or participate in each of the different markets.

name: Finance
description: This course serves as an introduction to the fascinating world of finance with a focus on investments. The aim is to provide students with a broad understanding of the various sub-areas in investments, including behavioral finance, market efficiency, market anomalies, sell-side analysts, mutual funds, and hedge funds. We will study how investors are affected by psychological biases and how those biases translate into anomalies in the stock market. We will ask how quickly the market reacts to public and private information. We will explore the impact of agency, information asymmetry, and social networks on stock analysts, mutual fund managers, and hedge fund managers. The course will be useful for students with an interest in financial research, investors, managers in financial institutions, and investment management professionals.

name: Corporate Finance
description: This course continues the journey to the world of academic finance, a theme that was begun in the introductory Finance course. The major objective of this course is to help participants develop a broad understanding of current corporate finance areas, including firm organization, the market for corporate control, corporate governance, capital structure, security issuance and payout policies. We will look at corporate finance theories that shaped the academia and industry. Research results from recent empirical work and their implications for research will also be discussed, where appropriate. Current issues in the financial markets will also be raised. The course will be beneficial for students with an interest in corporate finance research.

name: Adv Topic in Corporate Finance
description: This is a Ph.D. seminar class in corporate finance. The course aims to expose students to current and classic studies in corporate finance. The topics will be covered in the course including corporate liquidity management, executive compensation, the role of financial analysts, etc. I intend to discuss both theoretical and empirical papers.

name: Market Microstructure Theory
description: This advanced course explores theoretical frameworks that analyze how various (financial) securities are trade in different forms of financial markets – a topic often known as “market microstructure.” Students will engage with both foundational and cutting-edge research to understand the behavior of various market participants, the formation of prices, and the role of information in trading processes. Through rigorous qualitative modeling, students will develop a deep comprehension of the factors influencing market quality, like liquidity, efficiency, and stability.
areas: PhD Business Finance Advanced Research Topics

name: Investments
description: This course is an introduction to asset pricing and investments. We begin with a review of the theory of choice under uncertainty, and then develop classical asset pricing theory and investments. We also discuss empirical puzzles and recent theories that have been developed to try to solve them. Specifically, we will explore the mean-variance frontier and expected return vs. beta models and factor structures, such as the classic CAPM, APT, ICAPM, and the recently developed Fama-French five factor model and q-theory-based four factor model. We also explore equilibrium-based asset pricing model, such as the habit-formation model, the long-run risks model, and the rare disaster model. We will cover both equity and derivatives markets, as well as individual and institutional investments.

name: Fundamental Res. in Corp. Fin
description: This is a Ph.D. seminar class in corporate finance.  The class is an introduction to research on the structure of the corporation and its investment and financing decisions.  It is divided into two parts.  The first is about the theory of the firm.  It includes sessions on how productive activity is organized and how corporations in particular are structured to manage the agency problems that arise with any activity involving more than one person.  The second part is about the financing of firm activities.  It includes sessions on capital structure, IPOs, and payout policy.  We will discuss a mixture of theoretical, empirical, fundamental, and current papers.There is no text book for this class.  You are expected to have a basic understanding of MBA-level finance, however.  For review, or to answer questions about definitions and conventional thinking about a topic, please refer to recent editions of the textbooks by Brealey and Myers; Ross, Westerfield, and Jaffe; or Berk, DeMarzo, and Harford.Class sessions will be informal.  We will meet three times to discuss the readings in the list attached.  The amount that you learn in this class will depend heavily on your conscientious and careful preparation for the discussion meetings.

name: Finance
description: This course serves as an introduction to the fascinating world of finance with a focus on investments. The aim is to provide students with a broad understanding of the various sub-areas in investments, including behavioral finance, market efficiency, market anomalies, sell-side analysts, mutual funds, and hedge funds. We will study how investors are affected by psychological biases and how those biases translate into anomalies in the stock market. We will ask how quickly the market reacts to public and private information. We will explore the impact of agency, information asymmetry, and social networks on stock analysts, mutual fund managers, and hedge fund managers. The course will be useful for students with an interest in financial research, investors, managers in financial institutions, and investment management professionals.

name: Research Topics in Finance
description:
This is a Ph.D. seminar class in finance. The course aims to expose students to current and classic studies in various areas of finance and research methods. The topics which will be covered in the course will include the following, organized by instructor

Jianfeng Hu’s part
• Surveying empirical methods in market microstructure literature
• Surveying the options market literature (I)
• Surveying the options market literature (II)
• Surveying the real effect of derivatives literature
  
Chishen Wei’s part
• Measuring fund performance
• Role of institutional investors in corporate governance
• Identification: regression discontinuity, instrumental variables
• Measurement: connections, linkages, and networks

Roger Loh’s part 
• Surveying the sell-side analyst literature
• Surveying the asset pricing anomalies literature
• How to write a referee report 
• How to discuss a paper in a conference
areas: PhD Business Finance Advanced Research Topics

name: Corp Fin. Theory & Applied Res
longName: Corporate Finance Theory and Applied Research
description:
This is a doctoral seminar class in corporate finance. The class is an introduction to research on the structure of the corporation and its investment and financing decisions. It starts with the theory of the firm, which includes sessions on how productive activity is organized and how modern corporations in particular are structured to manage the agency problems that arise due to the interest conflicts of different stakeholders and the separation of ownership and control. The second part is about firm financing and investment activities. It includes sessions on capital structure, IPOs, and payout policy, as well as corporate social responsibilities. We will discuss a mixture of theoretical, empirical, fundamental, and current papers.

There is no text book for this class. However, you are expected to have a basic understanding of MBA‐ level finance. For review, or to answer questions about definitions and conventional thinking about a topic, please refer to recent editions of the textbooks by Brealey and Myers; Ross, Westerfield, and Jaffe; or Berk, DeMarzo, and Harford.

name: Corporate Finance II
description:
This is a Ph.D. seminar class in corporate finance. The class is an introduction to research on the structure of the corporation and its investment and financing decisions. The major objective of this course is to help participants develop a broad understanding of current corporate finance areas. It starts with the theory of the firm, with a focus on public firms, including sessions on how publicly listed corporations in particular are structured to manage the agency problems that arise due to the separation of ownership and control.  It is then followed by sessions on how firms are managed and financed, including internal corporate governance and the external market for corporate control, capital structure, and payout policies. We will also discuss issues related to the financing of private firms, the initial public offering (IPO) process and its legal content, as well as a stakeholder model with a focus on the tradeoff between shareholder returns and stakeholder welfare. We will discuss a mixture of theoretical, empirical, fundamental, and current papers.

There is no text book for this class. However, you are expected to have a basic understanding of MBA‐ level finance. For review, or to answer questions about definitions and conventional thinking about a topic, please refer to recent editions of the textbooks by Brealey and Myers; Ross, Westerfield, and Jaffe; or Berk, DeMarzo, and Harford.

name: WM– The ASEAN Context
description: The objective of this course is to introduce wealth management from a private high net-worth individual (HNWI)’s perspective with the goals of growing, protecting and passing on the wealth to future generations for HNWIs. Participants will be introduced to the current wealth management landscape in Singapore and the regions and hear from two panelists on their experiences identifying and addressing the needs of high net worth clients from China and ASEAN.  Next, we will focus on two popular investment strategies – real estate & REIT, and private equity.  Once again, we will hear from seasoned practitioners on their investment philosophy in these asset classes, and their investment process from prospecting, due diligence, selection to monitoring.  On Day 2 afternoon, we will embark on inheritance planning solutions starting with basic wealth planning solutions to protect and pass down wealth inheritance to next generations. On Day 3, we will examine more complicated structures such as trust and family office. We will use a number of real examples and cases to illustrate the concepts and bring to life real applications of the structures and solutions. There will be veteran practitioners who will share their expertise in trust structuring and family offices.

name: Pro-Seminar in Finance
description: The purpose of this course is to introduce area members’ main research topics and interests to the new PhD students. Each week, one or two faculty members will discuss their research work so as to expose new PhD students to interesting problems in the field. The key objective of this course is to jump start the matching process between students and PhD supervisors.

name: Corporate Finance
description: This course introduces the essentials of financial decision-making. The objective is to inculcate an understanding of the elements of strategic financial management and to build proficiency in the application to real world problems. Participants will be provided with a rigorous introduction to the foundations of business finance in competitive financial markets. The course is designed to equip managers and leaders with the basic tools that are necessary for managing a firm in a dynamic global financial environment. Emphasis will be placed on applying these tools to arriving at optimal decision strategies that will maximize the value of the firm.This course is a blend of theory and practice where the focus is on:1. Appreciating the financial environment that a firm operates in;2. Understanding the key drivers of firm value;3. Learning the underlying financial theories that drive practice;4. Maximizing value for a firm’s stakeholders.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Private Equity & VC Investing
longName: Private Equity and Venture Capital Investing
description: This course is aimed at providing students with a strong understanding of private equity and venture capital (“PE/VC”) as an asset class.  This will be important whether they pursue a career as private wealth managers, or join a PE/VC fund manager, or as founders/managers of companies which raise PE/VC funding, or simply to build on their investment knowledge and assessment capability.  The course will start off with an overview of the PE/VC industry, then proceed to examine the issues and skills from the perspectives of the fund managers, the investors in the PE / VC funds, and last but not least the companies seeking PE/VC funds.  Each session will start with a lecture followed by case studies and / or topical discussions. Emphasis will be on real life cases and issues, drawing on the Instructor’s 20-year experience as a private equity practitioner. Classroom participation is critical to the learning.
competencies: Valuation of Different Classes of Interest
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Hedge Funds
description: This course provides students with an overview of hedge fund management based on the instructors' investment philosophy and a \"Survivor\" framework. This framework provides students with an unified view of hedge fund management beginning with the setting of hedge fund objectives within institutional settings, followed by an examination of different hedge fund strategies, performance measurement, risk management and compensation issues. Case examples will be used to illustrate the how concepts within the framework can be applied.

name: Advanced Portfolio Management
description: This course seeks to provide a comprehensive coverage of concepts, theories, applications, decision-making rules in portfolio management via lectures & case studies. Topics include portfolio management for institutional investors, asset allocation decisions, risk management, execution, monitoring & rebalancing, & performance evaluation. A substantial portion of the course will mirror the portfolio management syllabus in CFA Level 3. In addition, specific research & case studies will be drawn from the financial industry to illustrate key concepts & good practices.

name: Advanced Corporate Finance
description: This course aims to provide students with an advanced study of Corporate Finance beyond the essentials. Students will be equipped with the necessary analytical tools to make sound financial decisions when exposed to actual complex situations. The course covers a wide spectrum of topics such as optimal capital structure, mergers & acquisitions, value creation for shareholders, IPOs, corporate restructuring, international investments and risk management. It will focus on: •	Understanding core financial tools that help students understand strategic and tactical financial problems •	Developing the linkage between corporate financial decisions and value creation in firms •	Sharpening the understanding of debt and capital markets as source of financing and value creation•	Providing a framework to help managers make optimal financial decisions
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Equity Analy. & Portfolio Mgt
description: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of equity analysis and portfolio management. Students will learn the concepts of return and risk, portfolio theory and capital market theory. They will learn the benefits of diversification through the formation of efficient portfolios. They will be introduced to asset pricing models such as the static CAPM, arbitrage pricing model and Fama-French 3-factor model. The course will expose students to the fundamental sources of value in a company and use these fundamentals to value its shares. The course will also touch on the portfolio management processes and asset allocation.

name: Merger & Acquisition
description: This course will illustrate the complexities and challenges of developing and executing M&A transactions in Asia.  Using actual case studies, we will cover all aspects of selling and buying into companies in Asia, from negotiation tactics to due diligence to valuation aspects. We will also analyse the challenges Asian companies face when they decide to expand beyond Asia through M & A.

name: Derivatives Analysis
description: This course will teach materials pertaining to the learning requirements of 2014 CFA Level I, II and parts of III under the topics of Derivatives. Most of the coverages are contained in the readings of CFA Level II. (In CFA syllabus, level I materials are mostly introduction to the operational characteristics and uses of the various derivative instruments of forward contracts, futures, options, and swaps. Credit derivatives under the generic types above are also an important category of derivatives in its own right. Level II and III contain some pricing and risk-hedging techniques.) This course covers the introduction to, the operational characteristics, and the pricing and valuation of forwards, futures, and options. (A later Advanced Derivative course in this MAF degree program will cover more detailed analytics of option pricing and hedging as well as swaps and credit derivatives.) Besides a pragmatic treatment of the subject including market details, aspects of practice including hedging and risk management using derivatives are also discussed.

name: Adv. Quant. & Econ Analysis
description: This course is relevant in the present times. 70% of global GDP is under 0 to 1% interest rates. There is resistance to the idea of interest rates being raised from 0.0%. Emerging economies see capital leaving the country. China’s economic future faces big question marks. Eurozone growth expectations are being scaled back and it is printing more money than before. The price of crude oil has suffered a large decline. Policies pursued in the developed world have disproportionate influence in Asia. Asian countries and other developing nations are forced to operate in a second best world. Emerging markets are forced to cut rates in boom times to discourage inflows and hike rates when capital flows out. They are forced to become a boom-bust economy.We need to be aware of the world of international finance, economics and policy and capital flows so that we are better prepared in personal, professional and policy worlds.

name: Fixed Income Analysis
description: Fixed Income Securities are securities whose income is literally fixed, and more generally any claims whose value or risk is related to interest rates and interest rate uncertainty. The course will cover the evaluation of these securities, the market operations and the risk involved. It then discusses how you can manage fixed income security portfolios and manage the resulting risk.
graduateOutcomes: Understanding of global and Asian perspectives

name: Investment Adv. & Wealth Mgmt
description: The objective of this module is to introduce the financial planning process and apply some of the tools to formulating an investment plan for managing, preserving and growing wealth for the individual. The body of knowledge in investment management has traditionally been focused on institutions. Institutions differ from individuals as most of them are tax-exempt, unlike individuals who are subject to various taxes. In addition, institutions have much longer investment horizons than individuals. Finally, the objectives and constraints of individuals are more varied than institutions. Hence, the tools and issues for investment management for individuals need to be expanded.  The formulation of an investment plan for retirement is used as a framework for discussing the various issues in investment management for individuals. Thus, we examine the key challenges and issues pertaining to ensuring that an individual has sufficient funds to live out his/her retirement years. Issues covered include taxation, asset allocation, insurance, annuities, pensions, housing, healthcare, demographics etc.As this is an emerging area in finance, students will not be learning a well-established body of knowledge but would learn how to think about the issues.
